en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
Victorious is Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, who gladdens the heart of Satyavatī.
The world drinks the nectar of speech that has fallen from his lotus-like mouth; may he,
who is like a mass of musk and whose very being provides protection,
be the earth for us through curds and milk, and may he be the liberation itself for the sake of our final release.
Janamejaya said:
Having regained the kingdom, how did my grandfathers, the highly fortunate Pāṇḍavas,
conduct themselves toward the great-souled Mahārāja Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
"How indeed did that king fare— bereft of ministers, bereft of sons, without refuge,
and deprived of sovereignty— and how did the illustrious Gāndhārī fare?
And for how long did my former ancestors remain [in that state]?"
"Those high-souled ones remain established in the kingdom; you ought to explain that to me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having obtained the kingdom, the high-souled Pāṇḍavas had their enemies slain."
Placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head, they protected the earth; Vidura and Sañjaya likewise waited upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
as did the wise Yuyutsu, that Kaurava son of a Vaiśya mother.
The Pāṇḍavas would consult that king regarding all their affairs;
permitted by him, they carried them out for fifteen years.
For those heroes always went and waited upon that king.
Having prostrated at his feet and remained steadfast in the will of Dharmarāja,
they were kissed upon the head by him and performed all their duties.
O King, he followed all of them in these matters.
Seeing them in such a state, Dhṛtarāṣṭra welcomed them;
and Kuntī, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, as well as Gāndhārī, Draupadī, Subhadrā, and the other wives of the Pāṇḍavas, followed her example.
They conducted themselves with equal conduct toward both mothers-in-law according to tradition.
There were costly beds, garments, and ornaments,
as well as all kinds of food and drink fit for a king in great abundance.
O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira offered himself to Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
likewise, Kuntī behaved toward Gāndhārī with the conduct due to a superior.
So too did Vidura, Sañjaya, and Yuyutsu the Kaurava.
They waited upon that aged lord of men, whose sons had been slain;
and he who was the beloved brother-in-law of Droṇa, a great and singular Brāhmaṇa,
Kṛpa— that mighty archer— was also present with him at that time.
And the blessed Vyāsa, that ancient seer, constantly dwelt with the king,
engaging in discourses concerning the celestial seers, kings, and *rakṣasas*,
as well as matters pertaining to dharma and judicial procedures.
Authorized by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vidura carried out those tasks;
even the most important and dear duties for his kinsmen were accomplished with very little expense,
indeed through the power of Vidura.

He performed acts of binding and releasing, as well as the liberation of those condemned to death; yet King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, never said anything at all. Furthermore, during his pleasure excursions, the Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira—
The one of great splendor granted all desires to the son of Ambikā. Cooks, confectioners, and makers of *rāga-khaṇḍava* likewise attended upon King Dhṛtarāṣṭra just as they had before.
The Pāṇḍavas, according to custom, presented Dhṛtarāṣṭra with costly garments and various kinds of garlands;
they also offered maireya wine, honey, meats, and light refreshments.
They prepared various kinds of colorful foods for him just as in former times;
and all those rulers of the earth who had gathered from every direction waited upon the lord of the Kauravas just as they had done before.
Kuntī, Draupadī, and the beautiful Satyabhāmā;
Ulūpī the Nāga maiden, and likewise Queen Citrāṅgadā;
the sister of Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the daughter of Jarāsaṃdha.
"O bull of the Bharatas, these and many other women,
all like servants, attend upon the daughter of Subala;
so that this man, separated from his son, may not experience even the slightest sorrow."
"Thus Yudhiṣṭhira constantly instructed his brothers," (15,001.023c).
Having heard these meaningful words of the King of Dharma, they then conducted themselves with particular distinction—with the sole exception of Bhīma. (15,001.024a–c)
"For that which occurred during the gambling match does not depart from the heart of that evil-minded Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that hero.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus honored by the Pāṇḍavas, the king, the son of Ambikā,
lived as he had before, attended by sages;
and that best of the Kurus bestowed gifts of land granted to Brahmins.
And King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, approved all of that; devoted to compassion and feeling great joy,
the king then spoke to his brothers and his ministers.
This lord of men must be honored both by me and by you.
He who abides by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is my friend;
he who acts contrary to it shall be my enemy and must be cast out.
On the days appointed for the *śrāddha* rites of his sons,
let the king bestow upon all of them whatever he desires to give.
Then that high-minded Kuru king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
He gave immense wealth many times over to the Brahmins.
And Dharmarāja, Bhīma, Savyasācin, and the twins as well—
all of them followed his lead out of regard for Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"How indeed might the aged king, though struck down by grief for his son,
not die upon encountering this sorrow caused by us?"—
for as long as that leader of the Kurus lives with his sons still living, there will surely be happiness.
"May he obtain those enjoyments"— thus they resolved.
Then all those five Pāṇḍava brothers,
being of such character, remained together under the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
And Dhṛtarāṣṭra beheld those heroes— who were humble, established in discipline, and always abiding in the conduct of disciples— just as a preceptor would look upon them;
and Gāndhārī likewise [honored] her sons with various *śrāddha* rites.
Having indeed bestowed his desires upon the Brahmins, he attained freedom from debt;
thus the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma and best among the upholders of dharma,
together with his brothers, honored that king.
Vaiśampāyana said:
That king, possessed of great splendor, aged, and the upholder of the Kuru lineage,
did not then perceive anything whatsoever unpleasant regarding the son of Pāṇḍu.
While the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were conducting themselves with righteousness,
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, became filled with joy;
and Gāndhārī, the daughter of Subala, likewise cast aside her grief for her sons.

She was always full of affection toward him, as if toward her own sons. O bull of the Kurus, the son of Kuru (Yudhiṣṭhira) always behaved only toward the king, the son of Vicitravīrya, in agreeable ways and never in disagreeable ones.
Whatever King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that lord of men, might say— whether it be a weighty or a trivial matter— and whatever the illustrious Gāndhārī says,
O great king, the king who is the leader of the Pāṇḍavas [does accordingly].
Having honored those words, the slayer of enemy heroes did exactly as he was told. That lord of men was pleased with his conduct,
yet he felt deep regret upon remembering his dull-witted and senseless son.
Always rising at dawn, having performed his prayers and being purified, the king would pray for the invincibility of the sons of Pāṇḍu in battles,
after having caused the Brāhmaṇas to recite benedictions and having offered oblations into the sacrificial fire.
That lord of men prayed for the long life of the sons of Pāṇḍu;
that sovereign of the earth did not find such supreme joy from his own sons as the joy he then obtained from the sons of Pāṇḍu.
O Bhārata, he then became very dear to the aged Brāhmaṇas, the Kṣatriyas, and likewise to the multitudes of Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
and whatever evil had previously been committed by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [was now forgotten].
Without taking that to heart, the king continued to follow the will of that monarch.
Furthermore, whatever man does anything unpleasant toward the son of Ambikā becomes an object of hatred to the wise son of Kuntī.
Out of fear of Yudhiṣṭhira, no man spoke even the slightest reproach regarding King Dhṛtarāṣṭra or Duryodhana;
for both Gāndhārī and Vidura were gratified by the fortitude of that lord of men.
O slayer of foes, because of his purity, Bhīma did not follow the conduct of Ajātaśatru;
yet even Bhīma, groaning, followed the king born of Dharma,
and upon seeing Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he was always ill at ease.
The Kaurava followed the high-minded Dharmaputra, the king who was acting according to dharma, even though his heart was turned away from him. Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, men perceived no difference in their affection between King Yudhiṣṭhira and Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; yet,
when the Kuru king began to think of his foolish son, [the situation changed].
Then, O King, that monarch harbored malice toward Bhīma in his heart;
likewise, O Indra among kings, Bhīmasena also could never tolerate Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the lord of men, and was always dissatisfied with him in his heart.

Both the Kaurava and Bhīma could not tolerate one another in their hearts; reflecting with subtle words, they each sought to overcome the other. Vṛkodara committed unpleasant acts against him that were not made public.
And they always returned his commands through agents who were mere pretenders;
for some years they conducted themselves in this manner, while he,
remembering his own evil counsel, observed their various actions.
"And he said this repeatedly: 'Those dull-witted ones are destroyed!
Then Bhīma, the indignant one, made a great sound with his arms in the midst of his friends, within the hearing of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī."
Remembering his enemy Duryodhana, as well as Karṇa and Duḥśāsana,
Bhīma then spoke these harsh words, highly incensed:
"The sons of the blind king shall be slain by me, whose arms are like iron clubs."
All have been led to that other world, their lives taken by various weapons. And he spoke this repeatedly: "Those dull-witted ones are slain!
These two arms of mine are like iron clubs, difficult to withstand."
Having come between these two, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have met their destruction.
These two of mine are stout and well-rounded, like the trunks of the king of elephants;
having encountered them in battle, the foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have gone to their ruin.
These two arms of mine, anointed with sandalwood paste and worthy of my veneration,
are those by which Duryodhana was brought to his destruction along with his sons and kinsmen.
O lord of men, these and various other such things have become thorns [to me].
Having heard those words of Vṛkodara, he fell into despondency;
urged by the arrows of Bhīma’s speech, he reached a state of dejection.
And that wise queen, who understood the passage of time, [spoke].

Gāndhārī, who knew all dharmas, heard those falsehoods; yet, observing Kuntī’s respectful service, she did not set her mind upon cursing her. Then, when the fifteenth year had passed, the lord of men—
Afflicted by the arrows of Bhīma’s words, the king fell into despondency;
and perceiving that Yudhiṣṭhira, though accustomed to comfort, was now intent on hardship,
the high-minded one resolved to perform austerities through the practice of yoga.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, did not perceive that;
nor did Śvetāśva, nor Kuntī, nor the illustrious Draupadī;
and the two sons of Mādrī, who were well-acquainted with Bhīma’s mind, acquiesced.
Guarding the king's heart, they said nothing unpleasant to him.

Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra summoned his circle of friends and spoke these words, which were exceedingly choked with tears: 15,004.014c Guarding the king’s mind, they said nothing unpleasant; 15,004.015a Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra summoned his circle of friends and spoke these words, which were exceedingly choked with tears.
With his body inflamed by the fire of Bhīma’s words,
the king, despondent in heart and filled with grief,
brought together the people along with the citizens and servants.
Desiring to go to the forest, he spoke these words.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"While the high-souled Pāṇḍavas are conducting themselves with virtuous behavior..."

King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, was filled with joy. "O Kauravas, it is known to you how the destruction of the Kurus occurred; you must understand that all of it was due to my own transgression."
I, who consecrated the evil-minded and deluded Duryodhana— the one who increased the fear of his kinsmen— in the sovereignty of the Kauravas; and I,
who did not listen to the meaningful words of Vāsudeva.
"Let this wicked and evil-minded man be executed along with his ministers," so it was said;
yet, overcome by affection for his son, he disregarded the beneficial advice offered by the wise Vidura,
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa.
At every step, this which was said by the Blessed One Vyāsa, the high-souled Sañjaya, and Gāndhārī, now torments me— namely,
that I [acted] toward the sons of Pāṇḍu, who are high-souled and possessed of virtues.
The elder brother of Gada, Janārdana, did not bestow this radiant ancestral sovereignty upon him,
for he foresaw the destruction of all kings; indeed,
he considered this to be the highest good.
Having approached that Lord of the Three Worlds and petitioned him,
I, being of very dull wit, shall now repent today for not having followed his word.
Thus, I have always turned away from these falsehoods of my own.
I carry within my heart thousands of things that have become like thorns;
indeed, I am especially consumed by distress during this fifteenth year.
For the sake of purifying this sin, I, though evil-minded, remain self-restrained.
"At the fixed fourth mealtime, or sometimes even at the eighth, I eat only for the sake of subduing my thirst; Gāndhārī knows this of me.
My entire retinue always thinks that I am taking food."

Out of fear of Yudhiṣṭhira, that Pāṇḍava is deeply tormented; he sleeps on the ground, devoted to silent recitation, covered with antelope skins upon *darbha* grass. And the illustrious Gāndhārī likewise dwells under the pretext of religious observances.
"My hundred brave sons, who never fled in battles,
have been slain; I do not grieve for those hundred sons who did not retreat in war, for they knew that to be the duty of a Kṣatriya."
Having spoken thus, the Kaurava addressed Dharmarāja:
"May it be well with you, O son of Yādavī; listen to these words of mine. I have lived happily, my son, being well protected by you."
Great gifts have been given, and ancestral rites performed again and again.
My life, O son, has been spent in excellence, and merit has been practiced according to my strength. This Gāndhārī, whose sons have been slain, gazes upon me with fortitude.

Those cruel men who wronged Draupadī and stripped you of your sovereignty have passed away; they have been slain in battle by the power of Dharma. O joy of the Kurus, I see no need for you to seek revenge against them.

15,005.017c All those who were slain facing the enemy have gone to worlds won by the sword. 15,005.018a But today, O King of kings, I must primarily act for my own benefit; you ought to grant me permission for that, as well as for Gāndhārī’s sake.

For you are the best among the upholders of dharma, ever devoted to righteousness; you are the king and the preceptor of all living beings. Therefore, O hero, I say this to you: with your permission, I shall take refuge in the forests.
"O King, wearing garments of bark and rags, accompanied by this Gāndhārī and bestowing blessings upon you, I shall become a forest-dweller.
O bull of the Bharatas, O dear one, this is the conduct appropriate for all of us in our lineage."

"O King, having entrusted the sovereignty to my sons at the end of my life, I shall go to the forest. There, O hero, dwelling with this wife of mine, subsisting on air or even remaining without food, I shall practice supreme austerity."
"And you too, my dear, shall partake of the fruit of this asceticism, for you are indeed a king;
for kings are the partakers of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds."—
Vaiśampāyana.
Having meditated with a swift mind upon his departure for the forest,
King Yudhiṣṭhira then spoke these auspicious words to that king.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, sovereignty does not please me while you are thus afflicted. Fie upon me, of such evil intellect, who am attached to the kingdom and negligent!
For I, O King, [have failed you] while you are pained by suffering and emaciated by fasting."
"Since I have been with my brothers, I have not found one who restricts his food or sleeps on the bare ground. Alas, I am a fool, deceived by you whose mind is so hidden;
for having first inspired confidence in me, you now experience this suffering."
"What use have I for sovereignty, or for enjoyments, or for sacrifices, or even for happiness,
O protector of the earth, since you have come upon these sorrows on my account? I know that both the kingdom and myself are likewise afflicted."
"O lord of men, by these words of mine who am suffering,
you are our father, you are our mother, and you are our supreme preceptor. For,
deprived of you, where indeed shall we remain?"
"O best of kings, let Yuyutsu be your legitimate son; O great king, let him be the king, or whoever else you deem fit. I shall go to the forest, while you rule this kingdom."
"You ought not to burn me further with infamy, for I am already consumed by it.
I am no king; you are the king, and I am dependent upon you.
How can I venture to grant permission to you, my superior, who are a knower of dharma?"

"O sinless one, there is no resentment in our hearts on account of Duryodhana; for that was destined to be so, and both we and he were deluded. Indeed, we are your sons just as Duryodhana and the others are."
In my view, Gāndhārī and Kuntī are indistinguishable.
O Indra among kings, if you depart leaving me behind, I shall follow after you; I swear this by my own truth.
"For this earth, girt by the oceans and filled with all treasures, would no longer bring me joy if it were bereft of you.
All this is yours; I propitiate you by bowing my head."
"O Indra among kings, we are dependent on you; let the fever of your mind depart.
O lord of men, I believe that which was destined to happen has now reached you.
By good fortune, as I attend to you, I shall release you from the fever of your mind."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dear one, O descendant of Kuru, my mind is set upon asceticism;
for it is indeed fitting for our lineage, O Lord, that we go to the forest."
"O son, I have dwelt here for a long time and have been served by you for a long time.
O lord of men, you ought to grant me leave, for I am old.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to Dharmarāja, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, trembling and with palms joined in reverence,
addressed these words to Saṃjaya, the high minister, and to Kṛpa, the great car-warrior.
"I wish for you to persuade the lord of the earth here;
for my mind is weary and my mouth is parched,
indeed due to my advanced age and the exertion of speech."
Having spoken thus, that righteous and wise elder king, the best of the Kurus,
suddenly fell into a state like one whose life had departed and leaned upon Gāndhārī.
Seeing the Kuru monarch seated there in such a manner, motionless—
The son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, the slayer of enemy heroes, quickly fell into distress.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"He whose strength was indeed equal to ten thousand elephants—"
This very king now lies beside a woman as if his life has departed—
he who, in former times, was so powerful that he crushed the iron image of Bhīmasena to pieces; yet now, seeking strength, he has resorted to a woman.
"Fie on me, ignorant of dharma! Fie on my intellect and fie on my learning, because of which this protector of the earth lies here, undeserving of such a fate!
I too shall fast, just as this teacher of mine does."
"If this king and the illustrious Gāndhārī do not eat," [said Dhṛtarāṣṭra].
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then the Pāṇḍava king, with his hand cooled by water..."
The knower of dharma gently wiped his chest and face with that auspicious,
fragrant substance, which was filled with jewels and medicinal herbs;
by the touch of the king's hand, the king regained consciousness.
15,007.001 Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Pāṇḍava, touch me again with your hand and embrace me.
Thus spoke Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was well-versed in the duties of kings, these auspicious words.
"O lotus-eyed one, I feel as if I am restored to life by the touch of you;
O lord of men, I wish to smell your head and to stroke it with both my hands, for my very life-breaths have not yet departed."
"O tiger among the Kurus, this is now the eighth mealtime for me since I last ate, which is why I am unable to move about. Furthermore,
I have exerted myself excessively in making this request of you."
Then, O dear one, my mind became despondent and I was as if deprived of consciousness.
But now, O Lord, descendant of the Kuru lineage, having received this touch of your hand— whose contact is like nectar—
I consider myself restored to life.
15,007.006 Vaiśampāyana said: O Bhārata, having been thus addressed by his eldest father, the son of Kuntī then gently touched him on all his limbs out of affection.
Then, having regained his life-breaths, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra embraced the Pāṇḍava with both arms and smelled the crown of his head.
Vidura and all the others wept, being deeply afflicted by grief.
Out of extreme sorrow, the Pāṇḍavas said nothing at all to the king.
But Gāndhārī, who knew the dharma, though bearing her grief deeply in her mind, restrained their sorrows, O King, and spoke thus: "Do not act in this way."
But all the other women, together with Kuntī, were deeply distressed; surrounding him with eyes filled with tears, they stood there. Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words again to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O King, O bull of the Bharatas, grant me permission for the life of an ascetic.
My mind grows weary, my dear son, as I speak again and again.
You should not trouble me further here, my son."
While that lord of the Kauravas was thus speaking to the Pāṇḍava,
a great cry of distress arose from all the women’s quarters upon seeing the king emaciated, pale, and in a state unbecoming of him.
Embracing his father— who was exhausted from fasting and reduced to mere skin and bone— the mighty-armed son of Dharma shed tears born of grief and spoke these words again:
"O best of men, O King, O scorcher of foes, I do not desire life nor the earth as much as I desire to do what is pleasing to you. If I am worthy of your favor, or if I am dear to you,"
"Let food be prepared first; then we shall know.
Then that king of great splendor said to the son of Dharma, "O son, with your permission, I desire to eat."
While Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of kings, was speaking thus to Yudhiṣṭhira,
the Ṛṣi Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, approached and spoke these words. Vyāsa said:

"O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, do without hesitation that which the high-souled Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the joy of the Kurus, has told you. For this king is aged, and especially so now that his sons have been slain."
"It is my thought that this hardship will not be endured for very long;
for the highly fortunate Gāndhārī, wise and compassionate,
bears her intense grief for her sons with great fortitude, O Great King."
I too say this very thing to you: do as I say. Let the king receive permission; let him not die here in vain.
Let this wise man be at ease among the forests fragrant with honey.
"Let the king follow the path of the ancient royal sages;
for all royal sages, in the end, take refuge in the forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed at that time by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds, the highly effulgent Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira replied:
"The Blessed One alone is our object of honor; the Blessed One alone is our teacher."
The Blessed One is the ultimate refuge for this kingdom and this lineage.
I am his son, and the Blessed One is my father, king, and preceptor;
according to dharma, a son remains obedient to the command of his father.
Thus addressed, Vyāsa, the best among the upholders of dharma and possessed of great splendor, spoke again to Yudhiṣṭhira, O lord of the people:
"O mighty-armed Bhārata, it is exactly as you say."

"This king has reached old age and stands at the ultimate limit of his lifespan. Having been granted permission by me and by you, O lord of the earth, let him fulfill his own purpose; do not be an obstacle to him."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, this indeed is the supreme duty of royal sages:
death in battle or death in the forest according to the prescribed rule.
O Indra among kings, by your father Pāṇḍu, the ruler of the earth—"

Having become his disciple, he attended upon this king like a preceptor; he performed great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees and adorned with mountains of food, he enjoyed pleasures, and he protected his sons.
While you were away in exile, this vast kingdom was entrusted to your son,
and for thirteen years it was enjoyed by him; various kinds of wealth were bestowed,
O tiger among men, and this king was served by you with devotion to his elders.
Together with his attendants, he has gratified both Gandhārī and the illustrious Kuntī.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, give leave to your father; it is now time for him to engage in the practice of asceticism, for not even the slightest trace of resentment remains in him.
Having spoken these words and taken leave of the king,
and having been told "So be it" by the son of Kuntī, he departed for the forest.
When the venerable Vyāsa had gone, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, then [proceeded].
Bowing low, he spoke very softly to his aged father:
"Whatever the venerable Vyāsa has said, whatever is your own opinion,
and what the great archer Kṛpa and Vidura have also said— "
"Yuyutsu and Saṃjaya as well—I shall do that directly. For all these men desire the welfare of this lineage and deserve my respect.
However, O King, I beg this of you with my head bowed low."
"Let food be prepared first; after that, go toward the hermitage.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the powerful Dhṛtarāṣṭra was granted permission by the king.
Then the wise king, followed by Gāndhārī, went to his own palace with slow and labored steps, as if rising with great difficulty;
on foot, that ruler of the earth was like an aged lordly elephant.
The wise Vidura and the charioteer Saṃjaya followed him, as did Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, that supreme archer. Having entered his residence, the king performed his morning rituals.

Having gratified the best of the twice-born, he then took his meal. O descendant of Bharata, the wise Gāndhārī, who knew the dharma, together with Kuntī and her daughters-in-law, ate after being honored with proper service.
When they had all finished their meals, Vidura and the others,
as well as the Pāṇḍavas, approached that king, the best of the Kurus.
Then, O great king, he spoke to the son of Kuntī in private.
Touching his back with his hand as he sat there, the son of Ambikā said:
"O joy of the Kurus, you must be vigilant in every way regarding the eightfold kingdom, O tiger among kings, placing righteousness at its forefront."

"But that kingdom, O dear son, descendant of Pāṇḍu, can indeed be protected; and as for dharma, O Kaunteya, you are wise—understand this. You should always attend upon those who are advanced in learning, Yudhiṣṭhira."
Whatever they may say, you should listen to it and act upon it without hesitation.
O King, having risen at dawn and honored them according to the prescribed rites,
you should inquire about your own affairs when the time for action has arrived.
O King, O delighter of the Kauravas, when they have been honored by you who seek the welfare of the kingdom, they will, my dear son, advise you on everything that is beneficial. Furthermore,
guard all your senses as one would protect horses.
They will indeed be for your welfare, like wealth that has been well-guarded.

You should appoint as chief officers those ministers who have passed the tests of integrity, who are pure by virtue of their fathers and grandfathers, self-controlled, and preeminent in all tasks; you should employ them in the highest positions.
You should constantly employ spies unknown to others to investigate your own kingdom and those of your enemies in many ways;
and your city should be well-guarded with strong walls and gateways.
It should be crowded with watchtowers and have six roads in every direction. Its gates should be constructed as sufficient and large,
well-distributed on all sides, and protected by mechanical devices.
O Bhārata, there is no need for men who are knowledgeable in worldly affairs and well-known for their lineage and character; rather, one must always protect oneself in matters of food and the like,
as well as during times of recreation, eating, and while using garlands, beds, and seats.
And your women should be well-guarded, supervised by elders who are trustworthy,
virtuous, of noble birth, and wise, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
and you should appoint as ministers brahmins who are experts in the sciences.
You should deliberate with those who are disciplined, of noble birth, skilled in matters of dharma and artha, and upright; you should consult with them neither too many at once,
nor all together, nor individually under some pretext.
Having ascended to a well-secured mantra-hall or a secluded spot, you should perform the recitation;
neither in a forest devoid of people, nor by any means at night. For monkeys and birds that imitate human beings—
All those who are dull-witted or lame must be excluded from the council chamber;
for it is my conviction that the faults which arise for kings from the betrayal of counsel can never be remedied in any way.
O King, O subduer of enemies, you should repeatedly speak of the faults of divulging secrets within the circle of ministers, and likewise of the merits of keeping them secret. And,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, you should ascertain the integrity or lack thereof among the people of the city and the countryside.
"O King, O subduer of enemies, you should act in such a way that this becomes known to all.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"My dear son, your judicial proceedings are always presided over by trustworthy men."

O King, these spies should be employed by those who are satisfied and well-disposed, and they must always be kept under control; O Bhārata, they should be men free from greed, not addicted to vices, affectionate, and equal to the king himself in spirit, who, having ascertained the gravity of the offense, inflict punishment upon those deserving of it.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those men should be led according to the law:
those who delight in seizing property, those who violate the wives of others,
those who are intent on inflicting severe punishment, and likewise those who speak falsely.
Those who revile, those who are greedy, those who kill, those who delight in violence, those who destroy assembly halls and pleasure gardens, and those who corrupt the social classes—
these should be punished with fines of gold or executed, according to the time and place.
One should avoid drinking liquor with servants in the inner apartments;
for when they are intoxicated, they utter insults, seize their wives,
even seek to kill them with weapons, and, being ruined and arrogant, they sport wantonly.
Various provocations clamor, and they do not know what is to be approached and what is not;
even a king, through excessive drinking, may destroy his entire treasury,
and he might bestow his collection of precious goods upon singers.

Having understood these faults of drinking, a wise man should drink alone with his own wife, openly and by means of skillful methods, for the sake of increasing his own virility. Indeed, at the very dawn, he should observe those who perform acts of expenditure.
Thereafter, you should provide ornaments and food;
then you should always look upon the warriors, gladdening them,
and evening time should always be set aside for your messengers and spies.

"O bull of the Bharatas, you should always devote the latter part of the night to the decision of affairs to be done; your recreation should always take place at midnight and at midday. Indeed, all other times are for urgent matters."
Likewise, at the proper time, you should remain adorned and bestow abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should not wear bracelets and other ornaments in vain;
rather, all auspicious items that destroy evil should be employed here at all times.
"O dear one, this cycle of karmas is indeed perpetual like a wheel. You should always strive to accumulate a treasury in accordance with justice,
O Great King, and you should avoid its two-fold opposite."
Having learned through spies of those enemies who are obstacles to your kingdom,
you should have them killed by trustworthy men at a distance, so that they destroy one another. Furthermore, O best of the Kurus, you should select your servants based on their past deeds.
You should have tasks performed by those appointed according to whether they are fit or unfit;
and, my dear, let there be a leader of the army for you who is firm in his vows,
brave, capable of enduring hardship, and a man dear to you.
"O Pāṇḍava, all the provincial subjects, the chief cooks, the members of the assembly, and those who engage in legal affairs— both among their own people and among others—
should observe your own vulnerabilities as well as the vulnerabilities of your enemies."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, you must always observe this:
even men who reside in other lands and are valiant in all undertakings should be favored by you with appropriate measures for their benefit.
"O lord of men, you who possess wisdom must bestow virtue upon those who seek virtue;
and they should remain as unshakable as the great mountain Meru.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
You should understand the circles of allies belonging to others as well as your own,
as well as those possessing neutral qualities and those who are intermediate; likewise,
you must understand all four types of enemies and those who are assassins.

O crusher of enemies, you must understand who is a friend and who is a friend of an enemy; likewise, O best of the Kurus, you must understand how ministers, the countryside, fortresses, difficult terrains,
and military forces may come under their control as they wish.
"O son of Kuntī, those twelve kings of various dispositions,
along with their principal ministers— these sixty and twelve qualities, O Lord—
are called a 'circle' (maṇḍala) by the teachers who are experts in policy."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, understand that the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) depends upon this;
O joy of the Kurus, one must discern increase, decrease, and stability.
O mighty-armed one, from these seventy-two [elements], the practitioner of the sixfold policy [proceeds].
When one's own side is strong and the enemy's side is likewise weak,
O son of Kuntī, the lord of the earth should then march forth after having declared war upon his enemies;
but when one's own side is weak, then he should resort to peace.
One's own side is weak, and even with the wise, it is then diminished; likewise,
a great accumulation of resources must be made.

O Bhārata, when he is capable of marching forth, that should be done without delay; at such a time, one should not divide the territory. O Bhārata, land that yields little fruit should be given to one who is the opposite [of a worthy recipient].
Gold consisting mostly of base metals, a friend who is impoverished and lacks a treasury—
one who is skilled in treaties should not personally accept these from those who act perversely.
And for the sake of a treaty, O bull of the Bharatas, you should seek to obtain a prince as a hostage.
But that which is contrary [to this], O son, must not be given by you under any circumstances.
You should exert effort toward his release, being skilled in means and counsel. And, O Kaunteya, the king should console the distressed subjects.
One must diligently assess the relative strength and weakness of calamities— whether they occur sequentially, simultaneously, or in pairs—
as well as their oppression, paralysis, and the depletion of the treasury;
all this while personally protecting one's own kingdom from enemies.
One who desires prosperity should not harm a neighboring king with whom he has entered into an agreement;
O son of Kuntī, he who seeks to conquer the earth should not injure such an ally.
You should, together with your ministers, apply yourself to the task of creating dissension among the confederacies.
By gathering the virtuous and likewise by restraining the wicked,
and never allowing the weak to be oppressed by the powerful,
you should remain established in the conduct of a reed, O tiger among kings.

If a powerful king should thus attack one who is weak, he should gradually turn him back by means of conciliation and other expedients. But if he is unable to do so, he should flee for battle along with his ministers.
By means of his treasury, the citizens, the army, and others who act for his benefit— yet,
if all these are unavailable, he should escape by the most capable [means] alone. By this sequence, there may be liberation, even at the cost of the body itself.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, best of kings, you should also consider here the matters of peace and war, which have two origins, three means, and many strategic alternatives."
"O Indra among kings, attend upon [the enemy] after having severed your own duplicity;
you should remember that the enemy is self-possessed and possesses contented and well-nourished forces.
However, at the time of attending upon him, the opposite procedure is prescribed."
O Indra among kings, at the time of crushing [the enemy], a withdrawal is then superior;
one should then cause the enemy's misfortune and division,
as well as their emaciation, terror, and great loss in battle.
A king who is about to march forth, being learned in the treatises, should reflect upon three things: his own power and that of the enemy— namely,
O Bhārata, the powers of energy, lordship, and counsel.
A man born [under such conditions] would go astray; otherwise, it would be the reverse.

A king should take up his forces: the hereditary army (*maula-bala*), as well as the allied army (*mitra-bala*), the forest-dweller army (*aṭavī-bala*), the hired army (*bhṛta-bala*), and whatever constitutes the guild army (*śreṇī-bala*).
In this regard, O King, the strength of allies does not differ from that of the hereditary troops;
it is my opinion that the strength of guilds and hired soldiers is exactly equal.
Likewise, O Monarch, the strength of spies is equal to each of the others.
When the proper time has arrived, O King, you must recognize what is to be known during times of exertion.
Furthermore, O lord of men, you must understand that calamities which befall kings, O Kauravya, take many forms; hear now about them individually.
"O King, O son of Pāṇḍu, there are many varieties of calamities;
a king should always strive to pacify them by employing conciliation and the other [strategic means].
A king, O scorcher of the foe, should set out on an expedition when equipped with the sixfold forces."
Equipped with the advantages of place and time, as well as forces and personal qualities,

a king who delights in the rise of prosperity should march forth when his troops are contented and well-nourished; furthermore, having been challenged, the monarch may march even outside the proper season.
That river had pillars of stone as its primary steeds and chariots, its banks and shores were covered with trees that were banners,
and it was filled with mud consisting of foot soldiers and elephants.
For the destruction of his rivals,
the king should advance; O Bhārata, O Lord, this is ordained in that treatise which Uśanas knows, concerning the *śakaṭa*, the *padma*, and the *vajra* arrays.

Having exhausted the enemy's forces and having instilled terror in their army, the king should engage in battle on his own territory as well as on the enemy's territory. Once victory is gained, he should pacify the region and station wealthy men there.
Having recognized that [the enemy] as his own domain, he should approach him with conciliation and the other [stratagems].
O Great King, one must by all means preserve the body in this world;
for both in this life and after death, one must accomplish the supreme welfare of the self.
Acting thus, O King, you shall hear auspicious words in this world;
likewise, by protecting your subjects with righteousness, you shall attain heaven after death.
Therefore, O best of the Kurus, you must conduct yourself in this manner for the welfare of your subjects.
"O dear one, for the sake of attaining both worlds eternally,
you have already been told this by Bhīṣma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vidura; yet,
O best of kings, I too must certainly speak it to you out of affection."

"O giver of abundant sacrificial fees, you should perform all this according to the proper rule; thus, being dear to your subjects, you shall attain happiness in heaven. A lord of the earth who might perform a thousand horse-sacrifices—"
Or, if one should protect the subjects according to dharma, one shall obtain an equal fruit.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O lord of the earth, I shall do exactly as you have said."
"O bull among kings, I am to be instructed by you yet again,
now that Bhīṣma has attained heaven, Madhusūdana has departed,
and both Vidura and Saṃjaya have passed away— who else is worthy to speak to me?"
"Since you, established in my welfare, now instruct me here, I shall do this, O protector of the earth; be at ease, O Bhārata.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the wise Dharmarāja, O bull of the Bharatas, that royal sage desired to grant leave to the son of Kuntī:
"O son, rest for now; even my strength is greatly exhausted."

Having spoken thus, the king then entered the palace of Gāndhārī. When he was seated upon his throne, Queen Gāndhārī, a practitioner of dharma who knew the proper time, spoke at the right moment to her husband, who was like Prajāpati himself.
"Permitted by that great seer Vyāsa himself,
and with the consent of Yudhiṣṭhira, when will you go to the forest?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Gāndhārī, having been permitted by my high-souled father himself and with the consent of Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall go to the forest before long.
For I am indeed the one who [provoked] all those wicked gamblers."
"I wish to bestow upon my sons wealth that shall follow them even after death. Having summoned all the subjects to his own residence,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke to them all for the sake of the funeral rites.
"O daughter of Subala, having taken my leave, I wish to go to the forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to the King of Dharma, the monarch sent forth [messengers].
And at his word, the lord of the earth brought all those things together.
Then, having emerged from that inner apartment, the king likewise summoned all his friends and all his subjects.
Then, having observed all those citizens and countryfolk assembled there, as well as the entire circle of his kinsmen who had arrived,
and the brahmins and kings gathered from various lands, [he spoke].
Then the immensely energetic King Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke,
while the Brāhmaṇas of Kurujāṅgala, as well as the assembled Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, listened with one-pointed minds.
"O sirs, you Kurus have lived together for a long time;
you are friends to one another and devoted to each other's welfare.
Therefore, what I shall now say, this being the present occasion—"
"Therefore, you must act upon my word without hesitation.
My mind is set on going to the forest together with Gāndhārī,
with the consent of Vyāsa and likewise that of the king, the son of Kuntī."

"May you also grant your consent; let there be no further deliberation among you. For this friendship between us and you is eternal, and it is my conviction that such [friendship] does not exist among kings in other lands."
"O sinless ones, I am exhausted by this age and likewise deprived of my sons;
I am emaciated by fasting along with Gāndhārī.
Now that Yudhiṣṭhira has obtained the kingdom, I have attained great happiness."
"O best of men, I consider the sovereignty of Duryodhana to be superior [to my own];
but for me, who am blind, old, and whose sons have been slain, what recourse remains?
O highly fortunate ones, save for the forest, you ought to grant me permission for that."
O bull of the Bharatas, having heard those words of his, all those people of Kurujāṅgala wept with voices choked by tears.
As they remained silent, devoted solely to grief and sorrow, he said nothing further to them.
15,013.022c Again, the highly energetic Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke this.
15,014.001 Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
15,014.001a Śaṃtanu protected this earth in accordance with what was right.
Likewise, Vicitravīrya, protected by Bhīṣma, ruled over you, O father; this is known to you without a doubt. Immediately thereafter, Pāṇḍu also protected the earth.
Just as my brother Pāṇḍu was dear to you,
he too protected [the kingdom] according to the law, as you well know;
for Yudhiṣṭhira was born immediately after his father.
"There is nothing here that shall ever prove false; this is my conviction.
O sinless ones, whatever service has been rendered by me to you—whether it was performed correctly or incorrectly—that should be forgiven by you with tireless patience, O highly fortunate ones."
And as for this kingdom that was enjoyed by Duryodhana without any thorns in his side— did not that dull-witted man of evil intellect commit an offense against you?
It was through the fault of that evil-minded one and the arrogance of the rulers of the earth.
A truly great slaughter occurred because of this misconduct of mine;
for the Kurus were slain and the earth was brought to ruin. Whether this which I have done be good or indeed evil, [let it be as it is].
"You should not take this to heart; you ought to grant me leave. This lord of men is aged, his sons have been slain, and he is sorrowful.
Considering that he is also the son of former kings, please grant him your permission."
"And this wretched, aged, and ascetic woman, Gandhārī, whose sons have been slain and who is afflicted with grief for her children, requests the same from you as I do;
for she knows these two elders to be likewise stricken with sorrow because their sons have been killed."
"Grant me leave— may you be blessed— and I shall go to you for refuge.
And this Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
should be regarded by all of you alike, in times of both prosperity and adversity."
He shall never at any time meet with adversity,
for he has four brothers as ministers who possess immense energy; indeed,
they are all like the guardians of the world and are perceivers of both dharma and artha.
He moves in the midst of the four world-protectors;
like Brahmā, this Blessed One is the lord of all beings and the entire world.
Thus is this mighty-armed one, surrounded by Bhīma, Arjuna, and Yama.
"The immensely radiant Yudhiṣṭhira will protect you.
Thinking that this must certainly be said, I speak to you:
Yudhiṣṭhira is entrusted by me as a deposit for all of you."
"O sirs, these sons of mine have been made by me as a trust belonging to this hero; if they have committed any offense against him,
you ought to grant me permission regarding that which belongs to me."
Indeed, you have never before shown me any anger in any way whatsoever. To you who are devoted with the utmost reverence, I offer this salutation with joined palms.
[As for those] of unsteady intellect, greedy, and acting according to their own whims—
"O sinless ones, accompanied by Gāndhārī, I beg all of you for this.
When the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra had spoken thus, those people of the city and the countryside addressed him as he was speaking in this manner.
With voices choked with tears, they said nothing; they merely glanced at one another.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by him, those people from the city and the countryside—
O Kauravya, at the words of the aged king, they became as if deprived of their senses. Then, seeing them silent with throats choked by tears,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the earth and protector of the world, spoke to them once again.
"O best of beings, I am old and my sons have been slain; together with this lawful wife of mine, I lament in many ways most piteously.
Yet I have indeed been granted permission by my father, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself."
"O sinless ones, that very person—known for his devotion to dharma by the king who himself knows dharma—is now seeking to dwell in the forest. Bowing my head again and again, I entreat you:
you ought to grant me permission, together with Gāndhārī."
Having heard those piteous words of the Kuru king,
O King, all the assembled people of Kurujāṅgala wept on every side;
they covered their faces with their upper garments and their hands.
Afflicted by grief, they wept for a moment like a father and mother;
with hearts become empty as they bore the sorrow born of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s departure, they became as if deprived of consciousness.
Having subdued that distress born of separation from the Kuru king,
they then gradually spoke their own opinions to one another;
thereafter, they all concisely summarized their words.

O King, having possessed a single Brāhmaṇa, they spoke to the lord of men. Then, O King, the aged Sāmba— esteemed, skilled in matters of state, and a master of the Ṛgveda— began to speak concerning his own conduct.
Having paid homage to the great king and addressed that assembly,
the bold and wise brahmin spoke to the king:
"O King, the entire message of these people has been entrusted to me."
"I shall tell you that, O hero; accept it, O lord of men.
O Indra among kings, O pervasive Lord, everything is exactly as you say.
There is not a single word of falsehood here; we are friends to one another."
In this lineage of kings, there has never been, at any time,
any king who was not beloved by his subjects while protecting them. Indeed,
you protect us just like fathers and like brothers.
O King, Duryodhana committed nothing improper;
striving to act for the sake of compliance, he did what was pleasing to everyone,
just as the sage who knows the dharma, the son of Satyavatī, has declared.
"Act accordingly, O Great King, for he is our supreme teacher. Abandoned by you, however, we shall remain for a long time devoted to misery and grief, O King, captivated by your hundreds of virtues."

O King, just as [the earth] was protected by King Śantanu and by Citrāṅgada, and by your father Bhīṣma— who was shielded by his own heroism— and likewise by Pāṇḍu, the ruler of the earth, who was endowed with your own wisdom;

Likewise, O King, your son has not committed even the slightest offense against King Duryodhana, who has protected him so well; rather,
they have placed their full trust in that lord of men as if he were their own father.
"O King, as is correctly known to you,
so it is: for a thousand years we have lived happily under the protection of the wise and steadfast son of Kuntī."

This righteous-souled king, who bestows abundant sacrificial fees, follows the conduct of the ancient royal seers who sustained your lineage— of Kuru, Saṃvaraṇa, and others, as well as the wise Bharata.
"O Great King, there is not even the slightest thing here that can be said against you;
we have always lived in happiness, protected by you. Not even the most subtle offense exists on your part, nor on the part of your sons."
"Regarding what you have said concerning Duryodhana in this conflict with his kinsmen, I shall also persuade you on that point, O joy of the Kurus.
The Brahmin said:
That the Kurus have come to destruction was not caused by Duryodhana, nor was it caused by you, nor by Karṇa and the son of Subala;
know that this was destiny, which cannot be overcome.
Fate cannot be overcome by human effort. O great king, eighteen akṣauhiṇī armies that had assembled together were destroyed in eighteen days by ten bulls among warriors.
O King, [he fought] with Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and others, as well as with the high-souled Karṇa, the heroic Yuyudhāna, Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
and the four sons of Pāṇḍu— Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins.
"O King, this destruction of men has been brought about by those compelled by the power of destiny. Indeed,
in this world, death by the sword in battle must necessarily be met by a kṣatriya, especially by one of the warrior caste."
By those tigers among men, endowed with both knowledge and the strength of arms,
this entire earth— with its horses, chariots, and elephants— has been subdued.
That high-minded son of yours, the king, has committed no offense.
That son was not the cause for the slaughter of those high-souled kings;
neither you, nor your servants, nor Karṇa, nor the son of Subala were the cause.
That the best of the Kurus and thousands of kings have perished is due to [the deeds of] fate.
"All this is indeed the work of fate; who here is able to say anything against it?
You are considered the preceptor and the lord of this entire world. Therefore, we grant you permission for your son, who is righteous in soul."
"May that lord of men, together with his companions, attain the worlds of heroes;
permitted by the foremost of the twice-born, may he rejoice happily in the third heaven. And you, O Lord, shall obtain merit and the highest standing in dharma."
O best of the Bharatas, he knows that very merit, the supreme goal in both worldly and spiritual dharma, and he knows merit in its entirety;
O mighty-armed one, he knows dharma, both that of the world and that of the Vedas.
We have witnessed the heroic deeds of the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men; even our mere glance toward them was not in vain. They are capable of protecting even the third heaven, let alone the earth.

O best of the Kuru lineage, O King, these subjects will continue to dwell with the Pāṇḍavas— who are adorned by their virtuous conduct— in both prosperity and adversity; and they will likewise respect the grants of land given to Brahmins, the endowments for religious purposes, and the various tax exemptions.
The son of Pāṇḍu indeed upholds the grants made by former kings;
far-sighted and perfected in wisdom, he is always like Vaiśravaṇa.
Furthermore, this high-minded son of Kuntī has ministers who are not base.

O bull of the Bharatas, he is compassionate even toward his enemies, pure, and upright in vision; the wise one always protects us like his own sons. Indeed, through association with that son of Dharma, he feels no aversion toward these people.
O royal sage, Bhīma, Arjuna, and the others will not act [otherwise];
for the Kauravas are mild toward the weak, yet like venomous serpents toward the fierce. These high-souled heroes, possessed of great prowess, are devoted to the welfare of the citizens.
Neither Kuntī, nor Pāñcālī, nor Ulūpī, nor the daughter of the Sātvatas will ever act with hostility toward these people;
for this affection shown by you has been further increased by Yudhiṣṭhira.
The people of the city and the countryside will not act with hostility toward them;
for the sons of Kuntī, those great chariot-warriors, being devoted to righteousness, will protect all men, even if they are unrighteous.
"O King, having removed this mental anguish from Yudhiṣṭhira, perform your righteous duties; salutations to you, O bull of the Bharatas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
All those people received his righteous speech, which was excellent in its subsequent qualities, saying, "Excellent!
Excellent! And Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having honored those words again and again, [accepted them].
Then, he gradually dismissed all his subjects.
Honored by them and gazed upon with auspicious looks, that king,
O bull of the Bharatas, with palms joined in reverence, paid homage to those people.
Then the king entered his dwelling together with Gāndhārī. Now learn what he did when the night had dawned. When the night had come to an end, the lord of men slept peacefully.
15,017.001 Vaiśampāyana said: When the night had passed, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā,
dispatched Vidura to the residence of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having gone there by the king's command, he of great splendor and the foremost among all the wise spoke to the imperishable Lord Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O Great King, Dhṛtarāṣṭra has consecrated himself for dwelling in the forest."
"O King, he will depart for the forest when this month of Kārttika arrives.
O best of the Kuru lineage, he desires some matter from you;
he wishes to offer a *śrāddha* for the sake of the high-souled son of Gaṅgā."
Of Droṇa, Somadatta, and the wise Bāhlīka;
of all their sons as well, and those who were his friends who have been slain;
and if you permit it, [the slaughter] of that lowest of the Sindhus.
Having heard these words of Vidura, Yudhiṣṭhira and the Pāṇḍava Guḍākeśa were delighted and honored them; however,
Bhīma, firm in his wrath, did not accept those words at that time.
Remembering what had been done by Duryodhana toward Vidura, the highly effulgent Phalguna, having understood Bhīmasena’s intention,
bowed his head slightly and spoke these words to Bhīma.
"O Bhīma, our aged father, the king, having consecrated himself for residence in the forest,
desires to provide the funeral offerings for all his friends. The Kuru prince wishes to give away the wealth won by you."
"O mighty-armed one, you ought to grant that request of Bhīṣma and the others.
By good fortune, O mighty-armed one, Dhṛtarāṣṭra now makes his plea;
behold the reversal of time regarding him whom we previously entreated."
"He who was once the lord of the entire earth, that king whose children have been slain by enemies, now desires to go to the forest.
O tiger among men, let your vision of him not be anything other than one of giving."
"O mighty-armed one, anything other than this would bring ill repute and be contrary to righteousness.
Attend upon your eldest brother, the king, who is your lord.
O bull among the Bharatas, you ought indeed to give, not to take."
When the son of Kuntī had spoken thus, Dharmarāja honored him;
but Bhīmasena, filled with anger, then spoke these words:
"O Phalguna, we shall perform the funeral rites for Bhīṣma here."
Kuntī will give [these gifts] to Karṇa for King Somadatta, for Bhūriśravas, for the royal seer Bāhlīka, for the high-souled Droṇa, and for other well-wishers as well.
"O tiger among men, the Kaurava king did not offer the *śrāddha* rites;
such is my conviction. May your enemies not rejoice;
may all those led by Duryodhana go from misery to even greater misery."
"By those scoundrels who have caused this entire earth to be slaughtered,
why do you today forget the twelve-year enmity and go into exile in disguise, thereby increasing the grief of Draupadī?"
Where was Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s affection for us at that time? Clad in a black antelope skin, stripped of your ornaments and finery,
you approached the king together with the daughter of Pañcāla.

Where were Droṇa and Bhīṣma at that time, or even Somadatta, when you lived for thirteen years in the forest on wild fare? At that time, your eldest father did not look upon you with the status of a father.

"O Pārtha, have you forgotten that which this defiler of his lineage, this man of evil conduct, said to Vidura during the gambling match, asking, 'What has been won?'? To him who spoke thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,"
The wise one spoke to his brother, rebuking him, saying, "Be silent.
Arjuna said:
"O Bhīma, you are my elder and my superior; I do not venture to say anything more than this."
For the royal seer Dhṛtarāṣṭra deserves honor in every way; the virtuous, best of men, do not remember offenses but remember good deeds,
for they are those whose boundaries of conduct and purpose remain unbroken.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Phalguna,
the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, spoke to Vidura:
"O Kṣattṛ, speak these words of mine to the Kuru king."
"O Lord, I shall give as much as I wish to give from my own treasury to my sons,
to Bhīṣma and all others, and to my well-wishing benefactors; let not Bhīma be dejected in spirit."
15,018.005 Vaiśampāyana said:
When this had been said, the King of Dharma honored Arjuna in return;
Bhīmasena, however, cast a sidelong glance at Dhanañjaya.
Then the wise Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words to Vidura:
"That king ought not to feel anger toward Bhīmasena;
for this Bhīma has been greatly afflicted by snow, rain, heat, and other such hardships."
"O wise one, you have experienced many kinds of sufferings in the forest; this is known to you. Nevertheless, at my word, speak to the king, that bull among the Bharatas, saying:
'Whatever you desire, and however much, let it be taken from my house.'"
"That which this Bhīma, being deeply distressed, performs out of stinginess—
this should not be taken to heart," so must that king be told:
"Whatever wealth I possess, and whatever is in the house of Arjuna..."
That king should be addressed as "Mahārāja," for he is the lord of all.
Let the king give to the Brahmins as much as they desire; let expenditures be made according to their wish.
Today, let him discharge his debt to his sons and his friends.
"O lord of men, know this: both this body of mine and my wealth are at your disposal, O Kṣattṛ; there is no doubt about this.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the king, Vidura, the most excellent in wisdom,
approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra and spoke these words of great significance:
"King Yudhiṣṭhira has been told your message from the very beginning."
Having heard those words of yours, that one of great splendor praised them;
and the highly energetic Bībhatsu offers his home to you,
along with whatever wealth is in his house, and even his very life itself.
"O royal sage, Dharmarāja grants you his kingdom, his life, and his wealth, as well as whatever else you may desire;
O Lord, Nakula and Sahadeva have also granted their permission."
But Bhima, the mighty-armed one, remembering his many and manifold sufferings, sighed deeply as if with great difficulty and gave his reluctant consent.
Thus he was addressed by the king, who is devoted to righteousness, and likewise by his brother Bībhatsu.
"Though entreated and established in friendship, the mighty-armed one [has acted thus];
yet the King of Dharma said to you, 'You must not harbor resentment,' for Bhīma remembers that enmity and would act unjustly."
"O lord of men, such indeed is generally the duty of Kṣatriyas;
Vṛkodara is devoted to battle and the duty of a Kṣatriya. And for the sake of Vṛkodara, both Arjuna and I [have acted] again and again."
"O King, let us both propitiate you, for you are the master here. O Ruler of the Earth, may your majesty grant whatever wealth you desire;
for you, O Bhārata, are the lord of our kingdom and of our very lives."
Let the best of the Kurus bring from here gifts of land granted to Brahmins, endowments for religious purposes, and funeral offerings for his sons;
let him also bring gems, cattle, female and male slaves, goats, and sheep,
and bestow them upon the Brahmins.
"O Vidura, by the king's command, have assembly halls constructed here and there for the poor, the blind, and the wretched, abounding in abundant food, juices,
and drinks; and provide watering places for cattle and whatever other various meritorious works there may be."
"Thus spoke the king and Pārtha Dhananjaya to me: 'You ought to tell us what must be done next in this matter.
Being thus addressed by Vidura, Dhṛtarāṣṭra then expressed his approval of that."
"O Janamejaya, on the full moon day of Kārttika, he set his mind upon a great gift.
Having been addressed thus by Vidura, the king then praised those words and reflected upon them.
Then, on the full moon day of Kārttika, his mind impetuously set out for the forest alone.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Vidura, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
became filled with joy at the deed of King Jiṣṇu.
Then, he [sent] handsome Brahmins, the best of sages, to Bhīṣma.
For the sake of his sons and his friends, he considered them by the thousands;
having prepared food, drink, vehicles, and garments,
as well as gold, jewels, gems, female and male slaves, and household furnishings.
That best of kings gave to the brahmins, repeatedly assigning them, blankets, skins, jewels, villages, fields, goats and sheep, ornaments, elephants, horses, maidens, and excellent women.
Having invoked Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Somadatta, and Bāhlika;
and King Duryodhana, and his sons individually;
and all his friends, headed by Jayadratha.
That Śrāddha sacrifice flourished, with abundant wealth in cattle as its sacrificial fee;
at that time, by the will of Yudhiṣṭhira, it was filled with a multitude of various riches and gems. Therein, men—calculators and scribes alike—labored incessantly.
At Yudhiṣṭhira’s command, they take leave of that king, asking:
"Give us your orders; what should be given to these men? Let it be granted.
At the conclusion of those words, it is seen that everything has already been brought right there.
When a hundred was to be given, ten hundred were given; likewise, when a thousand was to be given, ten thousand were given at the word of the wise King, the son of Kuntī.
Thus did that cloud-like king pour down showers of wealth.

He gratified those brahmins, just as a cloud saturates the earth with rain. Immediately thereafter, the lord of the earth, the king, flooded all the social classes there with a torrent of food, drink, and savory juices.
A vast ocean whose foam is cloth and jewels, whose sound is the resonance of drums, whose whirlpools are cattle, horses, and sea-monsters, whose great mines are women,
and which abounds in streams of villages and agrahāras, with gems and gold for its waters.
The ocean of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s compassion flooded the world.
Thus, O great king, he performed the funeral rites for his sons, grandsons, ancestors, himself,
and Gāndhārī.
When he became exhausted from giving gifts in great numbers,
that best of the Kurus then brought that sacrifice of charity to a close.
In this manner, that Kuru king performed the great festival of giving.
Abounding in actors, dancers, and female performers, and provided with abundant food, drink,
and sacrificial fees— having thus given gifts for ten days, O bull of the Bharatas, the king, the son of Ambikā, became free from his debt to his sons and grandsons.
15,021.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, at dawn, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā,
having prepared for their departure into forest exile, summoned the heroic Pāṇḍavas.

Accompanied by Gāndhārī, the wise king, having offered congratulations according to the prescribed rites on the full moon day of Kārttika, and having caused a sacrifice to be performed by Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas,
placed the *agnihotra* fires before him and clothed himself in bark garments and deerskins.
Surrounded by his daughters-in-law, the king then departed from the palace.
Following him were the women of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, as well as other women belonging to the royal lineage of the Kauravas.
At that moment, as King Vaicitravīrya was departing, a great clamor arose from them;
then the king [was honored] with parched grain and flowers.
Having honored that house with various offerings,
and having provided all his servants with wealth,
the lord of men then departed, leaving it behind.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, trembling with his hands joined in reverence, cried out loudly with a voice choked by tears:
"Alas, O virtuous Great King!"
"Where will you go? he cried,
and then, O dear one, Arjuna— the foremost of the Bharatas— fell to the ground, tormented by intense grief and sighing again and again.
Having said "Do not do this, Yudhiṣṭhira," Vṛkodara,
though himself sinking down, restrained him and supported him;
so too did the two heroes, Phalguna and [Bhīma].
The two sons of Mādrī, Vidura, and Saṃjaya,
along with the son of a Vaiśya and Gautama, followed them, as did Dhaumya and the Brahmins, their throats choked with tears.
Kuntī, carrying on her shoulder the hand of Gāndhārī— who was walking with her eyes bound—
then placed that hand upon the shoulder of the king.
The delighted Dhṛtarāṣṭra took her hand,
as did Kṛṣṇā Draupadī, the Yādava woman,
and Uttarā, the Kaurava princess who had young children.
Citrāṅgadā and certain other women,
along with the king and his daughters-in-law, set forth;
at that time, there arose the sound of those women weeping.
O King, like female ospreys crying out in grief,
the women of the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras then rushed forth from all sides.
O King, at his departure, the multitude of citizens in the city named after the elephant became exceedingly distressed,
just as they had been previously when the Pāṇḍavas were departing.
O King, during the gambling match in the assembly hall of the Kauravas,
those women whom neither the moon nor the sun had ever seen before were present at that time when the lord of men was there.
Afflicted with grief, they set out for the great forest where the lord of the Kauravas was going; they reached the royal highway.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O King, a great clamor arose from the women and men in the palaces, the upper chambers, and upon the earth. That king [proceeded] along the royal road, which was crowded with men and women.
In some way, the wise man, trembling and with palms joined in reverence,
somehow emerged; he departed through the Vardhamāna gate from the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura) and repeatedly dismissed that multitude of people.
Vidura had made arrangements to go to the forest together with the king,
as did the high minister Saṃjaya, the charioteer Gāvalgaṇi,
and he sent back Kṛpa and the great car-warrior Yuyutsu.
Having entrusted [the kingdom] to Yudhiṣṭhira, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
once the assembly of citizens had returned,
then desired to depart with his inner apartments, having been granted permission by Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Approaching his mother Kuntī, O bull of the Bharatas, he said:
"I shall seek out the king; you should turn back.
O Queen, it is fitting for you to go to the city surrounded by your daughters-in-law."
"Let this righteous king go forth, having resolved his mind upon asceticism.
Having been addressed thus by the King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), Kuntī, her eyes clouded with tears, then spoke as follows while embracing Gāndhārī.
"O great king, do not ever be negligent regarding Sahadeva.
For he is devoted to me, O King, and likewise to you at all times. You should always remember Karṇa, who never retreats in battles."
"For that hero was indeed defiled by me through my own lack of wisdom at that time.
O dear son, surely my heart is made of iron,
since it does not shatter into a hundred pieces even though I do not see the son of the Sun."
"Since things have come to this pass, O subduer of enemies, what can I possibly do?
This fault of mine has been made known to an extreme degree—that the son of the Sun was not [revealed]. For that reason, O mighty-armed one, you should bestow a supreme gift."

"O crusher of enemies, you must always remain together with your brothers for the sake of your eldest brother; O subduer of foes, you must always abide by what is pleasing to Draupadī. So too, O upholder of the Kuru lineage, must Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and Nakula."
"O hero, you must now take up the burden of the lineage; it has fallen upon you today.
As for me, I shall dwell in the forest with Gandhārī, serving the feet of my mother-in-law and father-in-law, living as an ascetic covered in the mire of dust."

Thus addressed by his brothers, that self-controlled and righteous-souled one fell into intense despondency and said nothing at all. Having reflected for a moment, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, [spoke].
Distressed and overcome with anxiety and grief, he said to his mother:
"What is this resolve you have made? You ought not to speak thus;
I do not give you my consent—please, show me favor."
O lady of lovely appearance, you formerly illumined us by inspiring us with zeal through the words of Vidurā; it does not behove you to abandon us.
Having slain the protectors of the earth, this kingdom has been obtained by me.
Having heard of your wisdom from Vāsudeva, that bull among men,
where is that intellect of yours today which was heard by me? For,
having spoken of your steadfastness in the duty of a Kṣatriya, you now wish to waver from it.

"Leaving behind us, the kingdom, and this illustrious daughter-in-law, how, O Mother, will you dwell in the empty forests? Be gracious to me! Hearing these words, choked with tears, from her son, Kuntī—
With her eyes filled with tears, she departed; Bhīma then spoke this to her:
"O Kuntī, when this kingdom was to be enjoyed by you as won by your sons, and when the duties of royalty were to be attained, why do you now have such a thought?"
"Why were we previously caused by you to bring about the destruction of the earth? For what reason do you desire to abandon us and go to the forest?
And why have you brought us children back from the forest?"
"O mother, these two sons of Mādrī are likewise overwhelmed by suffering and grief. Be gracious, O illustrious lady; do not go to the forest today.
First enjoy the prosperity of Yudhiṣṭhira, won through the strength of the sons of Pṛthā."
Thus, having made her resolve for dwelling in the forest,
she paid no heed to the various lamentations of her sons. Then Draupadī, with a dejected countenance, addressed her mother-in-law.
Weeping together with Bhadrā as she departed for the forest dwelling,
the highly wise lady, having made her resolve, went toward the woods while looking back again and again at all her weeping sons.
Then the Pāṇḍavas, along with their servants and the women of the inner apartments, followed her.
Wiping away her tears, she then spoke these words to her sons. Kuntī said:

"O mighty-armed Pāṇḍava, it is exactly as you say. O King, when you were despondent— having been robbed of your kingdom by the dice-game and fallen even from happiness— I previously offered this encouragement to you."
"I have offered this encouragement to you who were being humiliated by your kinsmen,
so that the lineage of Pāṇḍu, O bulls among men, might not perish,
and so that your fame might not be lost; for this reason, I have given you this encouragement."
"You are all equal to Indra, with prowess like that of the gods;
do not remain looking to the faces of others"—this is what I have done.
How is it that you, the best among the upholders of dharma, are a king comparable to Vāsava?
Furthermore, encouragement was given so that he would not suffer again in the forest;
encouragement was given so that Bhīma— possessing strength equal to ten thousand elephants and renowned for his valor and manliness—
would not meet with disaster.
"This younger brother of Bhīmasena, who is like Vāsava himself—Vijaya—must not falter"; thus was encouragement given. Likewise, Nakula and Sahadeva are both followers of their elders.
Thinking, "How might these two not perish from hunger? he offered words of encouragement;
and thinking, "Let this large, dark-complexioned, illustrious, and long-eyed woman not suffer in vain upon the floor of the assembly," that was also done by him.
Then, as they looked upon me— trembling like a plantain tree, in my menses, with faultless limbs, yet defeated at dice— Duhshasana, out of folly, dragged me about like a slave-girl.
At that very moment, I knew that this family was ruined;
the Kurus, my father-in-law and the others, were despondent when she,
seeking a protector, lamented like a female osprey.
O King, when she was seized by the hair by the evil-minded Duḥśāsana, my intellect was clouded with despair; however,
I provoked her in order to increase your majesty.
"O sons, know this from the words of Vidura at that time:
'How might this royal lineage not perish after obtaining my son? O son, it was for the sake of Pāṇḍu that I thus caused him joy."

"Neither his son nor his grandson, O King, shall ever obtain the worlds of the righteous from which his lineage has perished. My sons have already enjoyed the abundant fruits of my husband's kingdom in the past."
Great gifts were bestowed and Soma was drunk according to the prescribed rites. Yet, I did not urge Vāsudeva for the sake of my own benefit;
rather, that was done for the purpose of drowning out those lamentations of Vidurā.
"O son, O Lord, I do not desire the fruit of sovereignty won through my son; rather,
I desire the meritorious worlds of my husband attained through asceticism,
after having performed service to my mother-in-law and father-in-law as they dwell in the forest."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall wither my body through ascetic penance.
Turn back, O best of the Kurus, together with Bhīmasena and the others. Let your mind be fixed upon dharma, and may your heart be great."
15,024.001 Vaiśampāyana said: O best of kings, having heard Kuntī’s words, the sinless Pāṇḍavas,
filled with shame, turned back together with the princess of Pañcāla.
Then, O Bhārata, a great sound arose from all the women of the inner apartments as they wept upon seeing Kuntī in such a state. Then the Pāṇḍavas, having circumambulated the king, turned [to depart].
Having offered their salutations, they turned back without being able to turn Prithā back.
Then the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, spoke,
addressing and restraining both Gāndhārī and Vidura.
"O Queen, mother of Yudhiṣṭhira, let her be turned back at once;
for everything that Yudhiṣṭhira has said is indeed the truth.
Having cast aside this great sovereignty over her sons, which yields such immense fruit—"
Who indeed would go to the difficult forest, abandoning her sons like a fool? While remaining in the kingdom, she has practiced austerity, given gifts, and observed vows;
she is capable of doing so here today—listen now to my words.
"O Gāndhārī, I am truly gratified by this daughter-in-law's service. Therefore, O knower of dharma, you ought to grant her permission.
Having been addressed thus by the king, the daughter of Subala spoke to Kuntī.
He repeated all those words of the king and his own specific speech;
yet he was unable to turn back the virtuous Kuntī, who was devoted to dharma and had already set her mind upon dwelling in the forest.
But having perceived her firm resolve,
the Kuru women, seeing that the best of the Kurus had turned back, then wept aloud.
When all the sons of Pṛthā and those in the inner apartments had returned, [they continued their lamentation].
Then the highly wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra departed for the forest;
meanwhile, the Pāṇḍavas, dejected and overcome by pain and grief,
all entered the city in their vehicles accompanied by their women.
Hastināpura, along with its women, elders, and children, became as if joyless, silent, and devoid of festival;
and all the Pāṇḍavas were despondent, their hearts filled with resentment.
Deprived of Kuntī, they were afflicted with great sorrow like calves separated from their mother.
But on that day, the lord Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having traveled a very great distance,
made his dwelling there on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī.
The sacred fires were duly kindled by those foremost of the twice-born, masters of the Vedas and rich in asceticism, who shone here and there;
and that aged lord of men likewise had his fire kindled.

O Bhārata, having then worshipped the sacred fires and offered oblations according to the prescribed rites, that king stood in attendance upon the thousand-rayed sun as it reached the twilight hour. Then Vidura and Sañjaya prepared a bed of kusha grass for the king.
They prepared [the seats] for the Kuru hero not far from Gāndhārī. Then Yudhiṣṭhira’s mother Kuntī, established in virtuous vows, sat down upon the kusha grass in the vicinity of Gāndhārī.
Vidura and the others sat down within their hearing,
