as did the officiating priests, the twice-born according to their assigned places, and those who were followers; that assembly was presided over by eminent brahmins well-versed in the Vedas, and the sacrificial fires were brightly kindled.
That night passed for them like a night of Brahmā, increasing their joy.
Then, when the night had passed, having performed their morning rites and offered oblations into the fire according to the rules, they all set out in due order.
Facing northward and gazing [at the sky], devoted to fasting,
their dwelling on that first day was one of extreme sorrow for them as they lamented, being lamented in turn by the people of the city and the countryside.
15,025.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, abiding by the counsel of Vidura, the king made his dwelling on the pure bank of the Bhāgīrathī, a place fit for holy men.

There, O bull of the Bharatas, the Brāhmaṇas residing in the kingdom, as well as many assemblies of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, waited upon him. Surrounded by them, the king gladdened them with his conversation.
Having honored them according to the prescribed rites, he gave leave to his disciples. Then,
in the evening, that protector of the earth and the illustrious Gāndhārī approached the Gaṅgā and performed their purification according to the rules.
Likewise, O Bhārata, all the others, including Vidura and the rest, bathed separately at various sacred fords and performed all the prescribed rites there. Then,
the daughter of Kuntibhoja [Draupadī] approached her aged father-in-law, who had already completed his purification.
O King, Pṛthā led Gāndhārī to the bank of the Gaṅgā;
there, the sacrificial priests prepared the altar for the king,
and that monarch, true to his promise, offered oblations into the fire.

Then, from the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, that wise king, accompanied by his followers, self-restrained and with senses controlled, went to Kurukṣetra. Having reached that hermitage site, the intelligent monarch—
Then the royal sage approached the wise Śatayūpa;
for he had been a great king among the Kekayas, a scorcher of his foes, who,
having established his son in the sovereignty over men, entered the forest.

Accompanied by him, the king then went to the hermitage of Vyāsa. There, O King, he received that best of the Kurus according to the prescribed rites. Having received the initiation there, the king, the joy of the Kauravas, [proceeded].
Then he took up residence in that hermitage of Śatayūpa. O King, the high-minded monarch then explained the entire forest-dwelling rite (*āraṇyaka*) to him, with the permission of Vyāsa.
Thus, by means of asceticism, the high-minded King Dhṛtarāṣṭra then disciplined himself as well as his followers; likewise,
Queen Gāndhārī, clad in bark and deerskin, did the same.
O great king, together with Kuntī, she observed identical vows;
O monarch, having restrained the entire collection of her senses through deed, thought, speech, and even sight, she remained established in supreme austerity.
Reduced to skin and bone, with his flesh completely dried away, wearing matted hair and deerskins, and his limbs covered in bark garments,
that king practiced austerities there.
Like a great rishi, free from all defects and intense in his resolve, Vidura— possessing foremost intelligence and knowing both dharma and artha—
together with Sañjaya, attended upon that king and his wife.
Then, having conquered his self through terrible austerities, he, emaciated and clad in bark and rags, attended upon him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O best of sages, they went to see the king:
Nārada, Parvata, and Devala of great asceticism; Dvaipāyana with his disciples, and other wise Siddhas.
And the royal sage Śatayūpa, aged and supremely righteous— O great king, Kuntī performed worship for them according to the prescribed rites,
and those ascetics were also gratified by her service.

There, O dear one, those supreme ṛṣis engaged in righteous discourses, delighting the high-souled King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men. Then, during a certain interval in the conversation, the celestial sage Nārada [spoke].
He who sees everything directly related this story:
"In ancient times, there was a king equal to Prajāpati, free from fear from any quarter,
known as Sahasracitti, the grandfather of Śatayūpa."
Having entrusted the kingdom to his eldest son, who was supremely righteous,
the virtuous King Sahasracitya entered the forest;
the righteous lord of the earth, Śatacitya, entered the forest.
Having reached the culmination of his blazing asceticism, that high-minded lord of men attained the abode of Purandara. O King, I have seen that place many times before while traveling there.
In the abode of Mahendra, the king whose sins were burnt away by asceticism—
namely King Śailālaya, the grandfather of Bhagadatta—
reached the residence of Mahendra solely through the power of his penance.
Likewise, there was a king named Pṛṣadhra who was like the wielder of the thunderbolt;
that monarch also attained the vault of heaven from this world through his ascetic penance.
O King, in this very forest was also the son of Māndhātṛ.
King Purukutsa attained great perfection;
his wife was Narmadā, the best of rivers.
Having performed austerities in this forest, that monarch went to heaven.
There was once a king named Śaśaloman who was supremely righteous;
he too, having performed austerities in this forest, attained heaven. And by the grace of Dvaipāyana, you also have come to this penance grove.
"O King, having attained this supreme perfection so difficult to reach,

you shall depart. And you too, O tiger among kings, at the conclusion of your ascetic penance, surrounded by glory and accompanied by Gāndhārī, shall go to the destination of those great-souled ones."

O protector of the earth, Pāṇḍu constantly remembers you in the presence of the slayer of Bala; he will always unite you with what is most auspicious. And through your service, as well as that of the illustrious Gāndhārī, [you shall attain great fame].
"O King, your daughter-in-law Kuntī, the mother of Yudhiṣṭhira— for he is eternal Dharma— shall go to the same world as her husband;
we perceive this, O monarch, with our divine vision."
The high-souled Vidura shall enter into Yudhiṣṭhira,
and Sañjaya, purified by his meditation upon you, shall attain heaven. Having heard this, the high-souled lord of the Kauravas—
Together with his wife, the wise king, being pleased, accepted Nārada’s words and, having praised them,
offered incomparable worship to Nārada.
Likewise, O King, all those assemblies of brahmins honored Nārada exceedingly out of affection for King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, being greatly delighted again and again, those best of the twice-born praised those words of Nārada. Vaiśampāyana said: "The best of the twice-born indeed praised that speech of Nārada."
The royal sage Śatayūpa then addressed these words to Nārada:
"O illustrious one of great splendor, the faith of the Kuru king, as well as that of all these people and myself, has been increased by your holiness!"
"O celestial sage, honored by the world, I have a certain intention to speak; listen as I declare it concerning King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
You, through your divine vision, are one who knows the truth of every occurrence."
"O divine sage, you who are disciplined perceive the various destinies of men;
you have spoken of the worlds of great Indra for those kings,
but the worlds of this king have not been mentioned by you, O great muni."

"O Lord, I wish to hear from you what the status of this lord of the earth is—of what nature and when it occurred; tell that to me who asks. Thus addressed by him, Nārada spoke words that were pleasing to the minds of all.
15,027.007c The one of divine vision and great asceticism spoke in the midst of the virtuous:
15,027.008a "O royal sage, having gone by chance to the abode of Śakra, I beheld there Śakra, the lord of Śacī, and the king of men, Pāṇḍu."

There, O King, this conversation concerning Dhṛtarāṣṭra took place, as he sat upon half of Indra’s throne together with Mādrī— the Great-Souled One who was augmented by the merit performed by his virtuous sons, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others.
"O King, regarding this king who performs such difficult penance,
I heard this from Śakra as he was speaking:
three years remain of this king's maximum lifespan."
Then, accompanied by Gāndhārī, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra— honored by the king of kings— shall sport in the abode of Kubera,
adorned with divine ornaments and traveling in a celestial chariot that moves at will.
"The illustrious son of a seer, whose sins have been consumed by austerity,
shall wander at will through the worlds of the gods, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas;
this is the righteous soul about whom you asked me."
"Out of affection, I have joyfully recounted this great secret of the gods to you,
for you possess the wealth of sacred learning and have burnt away all sins through austerity.
Having heard these sweet words of the celestial sage, they [responded].
All became cheerful and delighted, as did that king.
Having thus attended upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra with such discourses, those wise men,
established in the path of the Siddhas, departed according to their pleasure.
15,028.001 Vaiśampāyana said: 15,028.001a When the lord of the Kauravas had gone to the forest, O King, the Pāṇḍavas became struck by pain and grief, and were afflicted by sorrow for their mother.
Likewise, all the citizens sat grieving for the lord of men,
while the Brahmins there engaged in conversations concerning the king;
indeed, in various places, there were discussions among the twice-born regarding the Kauravas.
"How indeed does that aged king dwell in the desolate forest?
And how does the highly fortunate Gāndhārī, and Pṛthā Kuntī, dwell there?
For that royal sage deserves happiness; that great forest is not a place of happiness."
In what state was he when he encountered [this], his wisdom-eye destroyed and his sons slain? Kuntī, not seeing her sons, performed a most difficult deed:
she renounced royal splendor and chose a life in the forest.

And what is the condition of Vidura, the self-controlled one who is devoted to serving his brother? And how is that wise son of Gavalgaṇa, who remains faithful to the sustenance provided by his master?
Furthermore, from their childhood, the citizens have been struck down by anxiety and grief.
Meeting one another here and there, they all engaged in conversation;
and all those Pāṇḍavas, being deeply overcome by grief,
remained in the city for no very long time, mourning for their aged mother.
In the same way, as they reflected upon their aged father, the lord of men whose sons had been slain,
and upon the highly fortunate Gāndhārī and the high-minded Vidura,
no joy arose within them at that time.
Neither in sovereignty, nor among women, nor likewise in the study of the Vedas did they find supreme satisfaction; rather, they fell into utter despondency as they reflected upon the king,
repeatedly recollecting that terrible slaughter of their kinsmen.
The destruction of the youth Abhimanyu at the forefront of battle,
as well as that of the mighty-armed Karṇa who never fled from combat,
and likewise of the sons of Draupadī and other friends as well.

Remembering that slaughter, those heroes became dejected in spirit. O Bhārata, constantly reflecting upon the earth whose preeminent warriors had been slain and whose jewels had been destroyed, they found no sleep.
Draupadī, whose sons had been slain, and the beautiful Subhadrā—
those two queens were then neither joyful nor delighted, remaining dejected.
But seeing the son of Vairāṭī, your father Parikṣit, [they were moved].
Your ancestors held onto their lives,
though they were struck by the force of grief and deprived of their senses day after day along with those city-dwellers.
Having abandoned their enjoyments and crushed the kingdoms of others, they remained there with focused devotion, having renounced all desires.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus those tigers among men, the heroic Pāṇḍavas, the delighters of their mother,
became deeply afflicted with grief as they remembered their mother,
they who had formerly been constantly occupied with the affairs of state.
At that time, they performed no royal duties anywhere in the city;
as if possessed by grief, they took no pleasure in anything. Even when addressed, they did not respond with any courtesy whatsoever.
Those heroes, invincible and like the ocean in depth,
their discernment struck by grief, became as if they had lost consciousness;
then those descendants of Kuru began to remember their mother.
"How indeed does the emaciated Pṛthā carry her aged parents today?
And how does that protector of the earth, his sons slain and left without refuge, dwell alone with his wife in the forest infested by beasts of prey?"
"And how does that illustrious queen Gāndhārī, whose kinsmen have been slain,
follow her blind and aged husband into the lonely forest?
As they were speaking thus, a sense of longing then arose within them.
His mind was set upon departing out of a desire to see Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then Sahadeva, having prostrated before the king, spoke these words:
"Oh, your heart has been seen by me regarding this journey!"

"O Indra among kings, it was not out of disrespect that I was unable to speak of your departure myself; rather, this very matter has now presented itself. By good fortune, I shall see Kuntī, that ascetic woman, as she carries on her life."

"When shall I see my mother— once grown up in palaces and mansions, destined for the utmost happiness, now an aged female ascetic with matted hair, her body scarred by *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass, exhausted and deeply afflicted by sorrow?"
"O bull of the Bharatas, the destinies of mortals are indeed transient,
since Kuntī, a princess, dwells there in the forest in misery. Having heard these words of Sahadeva, Draupadī, the best of women, [spoke].
Having honored and greeted the king, the queen said:
"When shall I see that lady Pṛthā, if she still lives? For if she is alive today, O lord of men, we shall find great joy."
"May this resolve be yours forever, and may your mind delight in dharma,
O Indra among kings, since today you will unite us with what is most beneficial.
And know, O King, that these women stand here with their feet upon the threshold."
"Desiring the sight of Kuntī, Gāndhārī, and his father-in-law"—
having been addressed thus by Queen Pāñcālī, O bull of the Bharatas,
that king summoned all the commanders of the army and then spoke as follows.
"Dispatch my army, abounding in chariots and elephants!
I shall see King Dhṛtarāṣṭra dwelling in the forest.
Then the king spoke to the superintendents of the women regarding his various vehicles.
"Let thousands of palanquins be prepared;
let the wagons, market-stalls, tents, treasuries, and artisans set forth,
as well as the treasury-keepers, toward the hermitage at Kurukṣetra."
"And whatever citizen desires to see the king, let him go unhindered, well-prepared, and well-protected. Likewise,
let the cooks, the kitchen supervisors, and the entire kitchen staff [proceed]."
"Let various kinds of food and edibles be carried by my carts;
let the departure be proclaimed for tomorrow morning without delay,
and let diverse dwellings be constructed along the road this very day."
Having thus given his command, that Pāṇḍava king, together with his brothers,
set out on the following day, preceded by women and children.
He remained outside for several days in this manner, protecting the vast multitude of people.
The king dwelt there for fifteen years and two months, and then he departed for the forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then that best of the Bharatas gave orders to the army.
Protected by men led by Arjuna who were like the guardians of the world, a great sound of joy arose from the horsemen there as they cried out, "Yoke! Yoke! and "Be harnessed! Be harnessed!"
Some men went by vehicles, some on horses swift as thought,
and others on chariots shaped like cities that resembled blazing fires;
likewise, O lord of men, some went on great elephants and others on camels.
Likewise, other foot-soldiers who fought with claws and spears,
as well as the people of the city and the countryside in various kinds of vehicles,
followed the Kuru king out of a desire to see Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
And at the king’s command, the preceptor Gautama Kṛpa,
taking the army, set out for the hermitage as its commander.
Then the illustrious Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus, was surrounded by the twice-born brahmins.
Being praised by many bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists,
with a white parasol held over his head,
the joy of the Kurus set forth with a great array of chariots.
Vṛkodara, whose deeds are terrible, the son of Māruta, set forth with elephants resembling mountains, equipped with ready machines and weapons;
likewise, the two sons of Mādrī also proceeded, well-surrounded by horsemen.
15,030.010c Those two, who inspired joy and were equipped with armor and banners,
advanced. 15,030.011a And the self-controlled Arjuna, of great splendor, followed the king in a chariot as radiant as the sun, yoked with divine white horses.
The throngs of women, led by Draupadī, set out in palanquins accompanied by the female superintendents, distributing immeasurable wealth; the procession was filled with abundant men,
elephants, and horses, and resounded with the music of flutes and lutes.
O bull of the Bharatas, that army of the Pāṇḍavas then shone brightly;
O lord of the people, having made their halts in succession at delightful riverbanks and lakes, those bulls of the Kurus proceeded on their way.
The highly energetic Yuyutsu and the domestic priest Dhaumya,
at the command of Yudhiṣṭhira, undertook the protection of the city.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira descended upon Kurukṣetra.
Having crossed the supremely purifying river Yamunā in due order,
O Kauravya, he saw from afar the hermitage of that wise royal seer Śatayūpa and also that of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, all the people, filled with great joy, entered that forest directly, filling it with loud shouts. Vaiśampāyana said:
Then those Pāṇḍavas, having dismounted from their vehicles at a distance and proceeding on foot, approached the hermitage of the king, bowing low with humility.
And all those citizens, as well as the inhabitants of the kingdom, [did the same].
Then the women of the Kuru chiefs followed on foot.
Thereupon the Pāṇḍavas went to the hermitage of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
which was empty, crowded with herds of deer, and adorned with groves of plantain trees.
Then, ascetics observing various vows gathered there,
filled with curiosity, desiring to see the arrived Pāṇḍavas.
Thereupon the king asked them, "Where is that upholder of the Kuru lineage?"
"O Lord, our eldest father has gone away," he said, overwhelmed with tears.
Then they spoke these words to him: "He has gone for the sake of flowers and a water-pot to plunge into the Yamunā."
Then, by the path described by them, they set out;
and not far away, those on foot beheld them all. Then, longing for the sight of their father, they proceeded with haste.
But Sahadeva ran with speed toward where Pṛthā was;
weeping aloud, the wise youth touched his mother’s feet,
and she, her face clouded with tears, beheld her beloved son.
Embracing his son with both arms and lifting him up,
he announced to Gāndhārī that Sahadeva had arrived;
immediately after, [he announced] the king, Bhīmasena, and then Arjuna.
Seeing Nakula, Pṛthā hurried forward;
for she had gone ahead of that couple whose sons had been slain.
As they dragged her along, seeing her, they collapsed upon the ground.
O King, they fell at the feet of those two whose sons had been slain. Recognizing them by their voices and by touch, the high-minded and wise lord, the king, comforted them.
Then, shedding tears, those high-souled ones approached the king together with Gāndhārī and their mother according to the prescribed rites;
at that time, they themselves took up the water-pitchers for all of them.
15,031.015c Then the Pāṇḍavas regained consciousness and were comforted once more by their mother.
15,031.016a Thereupon, the wives of those lions among men, as well as the host of warriors,
and the citizens and countryfolk, beheld that lord of men.

Then King Yudhiṣṭhira announced those people by their names and lineages, and he honored them in return. Surrounded by them, his eyes clouded with tears of joy, he felt as though he were truly himself.

The wise king, together with Gāndhārī and Kuntī, was greeted by his daughters-in-law, headed by Kṛṣṇā, as he stood in his palace just as before in the city of Hastināpura; and he returned their greetings with joy.
Then he arrived at the hermitage frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
crowded with those desiring to see him, like the sky filled with hosts of stars.
Vaiśampāyana said:

O bull of the Bharatas, that king, together with those tigers among men— his brothers who possessed beautiful lotus-like eyes— and with highly fortunate ascetics gathered from various lands, then took his seat in that hermitage.
15,032.002c To see the sons of the Kuru king, the broad-chested Pāṇḍavas,
15,032.003a they said, "We wish to know which among these is Yudhiṣṭhira,
and likewise Bhīma, Arjuna, the Yamas, and the illustrious Draupadī."
Then Sūta Sañjaya announced them all by their names,
as well as Draupadī and all the other Kuru women.
"This one, who is fair-complexioned like pure gold..."
With a body like that of a full-grown great lion,
possessing a formidable nose and large, long eyes, and with a copper-colored, broad face— this is the King of the Kurus.
Furthermore, he walks with the gait of a lordly elephant in rut;
he is as pure and fair as refined gold;
his shoulders are broad and expansive, and his arms are large and long.
"Vṛkodara, look, look at him!
And this dark-complexioned youth by his side, a great archer who resembles the leader of a herd of elephants— "
With shoulders as high as a lion’s and a gait like that of a sporting elephant,
this hero Arjuna has eyes as broad as lotuses;
these two best of men stand near Kuntī.
These two twins, who are like Viṣṇu and Mahendra,
have no equal in the entire world of men, whether in form, in strength, or in character.
Furthermore, this woman with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
her youth barely touching middle age,
possessing the luster of a blue lotus, is like the presiding deity of the city.
Kṛṣṇā stood there like Lakṣmī incarnate;
by her side was this Gaurī, possessing the luster of the finest gold, appearing as if she were Splendor itself in bodily form.
Standing in the midst [of them] is this sister of that peerless wielder of the discus, O best of the twice-born;
she is as fair as pure Jāmbūnada gold.
The wife of Pārtha was the daughter of the lord of serpents,
and Citrāṅgadā was the daughter of a king; she who [is adorned] with the foremost of flowers, the *savarṇā*, *madhūka*, and *puṣpa*.
This sister of the commander of the royal army,
whose complexion was like a garland of full-blown blue lotuses,
always rivaled Kṛṣṇa, O King.
This foremost prize belongs to Vṛkodara,
and she is the daughter of the king of Magadha,
known as Jarāsaṃdha.
The wife of the younger son of Mādravatī was considered as fair as a garland of campaka flowers;
she stood there with a body dark like a blue lotus.
This woman, who sits nearby upon the ground,
is considered the wife of the son of Mādravatī; she is the lotus-eyed elder sister of that youth.
This woman, fair as refined gold, is the daughter of King Virāṭa accompanied by her son;
she is the wife of Abhimanyu, who was slain in battle.
Deprived of his chariot by those men, Droṇa and the others, who remained upon their own chariots—
these wives of the king of men, with their hair disheveled down to their parted lines and wearing white upper garments.
This aged king has more than a hundred daughters-in-law who are now heroless, their husbands and protectors having been slain. These have been described to you according to their principal ones.
Due to their Brahmin nature,
all these wives of the king— possessing upright intellects and pure beings, and being of perfectly purified essence— were questioned by you.
Thus that king, the best of the Kuru elders,
having met with those sons of gods among men,
then inquired after the welfare of them all.
Then, when all the ascetics and the warriors had departed,
having released their mounts and left behind that circle of hermitages, they settled down.
When the women, the elderly, and the children were well-seated,
he inquired after their welfare according to their rank.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:

"O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, my dear son, I hope you are well, together with all your brothers as well as the people of the city and the countryside? And those who depend upon you for their livelihood— do they also remain free from affliction?"
O Lord, do your ministers, your groups of servants,
and your elders also dwell free from fear within your realm?
And do you abide by the ancient code of conduct practiced by the royal seers?
I hope that by not interrupting your inheritance, your treasury is being replenished;
that you conduct yourself appropriately toward enemies, neutrals, and allies;
and that you properly honor the Brahmins with land grants.
O bull among the Bharatas, are your enemies, your elders, the citizens, your servants, or even your own kinsmen satisfied with your conduct?
O Indra among kings, do you, full of faith, perform sacrifices for the ancestors and the gods?
O Bhārata, do you honor guests with food and drink? And in your realm, are the Brahmins devoted to their own duties—
whether they be Kṣatriyas, members of the Vaiśya class, or even Śūdra householders?

"O bull among men, do all those hermitages, castes, and those established in dharma who possess wealth remain secure? I hope that you do not grieve for, nor beg from, women, children, or the elderly; and I hope that your female relatives are honored in your home."
"O Great King, having obtained you as its sovereign, does this lineage of royal seers not suffer in reputation, but rather thrives as is fitting? Vaiśampāyana said:
To him who was speaking thus, he who was skilled in the art of speech and knowledgeable in logic replied with words joined by inquiries after his welfare:
"O King, does your asceticism flourish, now that your exertion is slight?"
"O King, will this mother of mine also serve you without weariness? And will her dwelling in the forest become fruitful?
This elder mother of mine is exhausted by the wind and the journey."

"Endowed with terrible ascetic power, does the Goddess not grieve for her sons of great heroism who were devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriyas? And does she perhaps never think ill of us, those constant evildoers?"
"O King, where is that Vidura? We do not see him.
Is this Sañjaya well, and is he indeed established in ascetic penance?
Thus addressed, Dhṛtarāṣṭra replied to the lord of men as follows.
"O son, Vidura is well; he has undertaken severe asceticism.
Subsisting on air, taking no food at all, emaciated and covered with veins, he is occasionally seen by the brahmins somewhere in this empty forest."
While he was speaking thus, the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra— matted-haired, with a mouthful of betel, and emaciated—
departed for the forest; so too did that king, the Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira.
There Vidura was seen, O lord of the earth,
appearing from afar as the Kṣattṛ described to the king: naked, his limbs smeared with filth, and covered with the dust of the forest.
But Vidura, whose soul is righteous, seeing the people, turned back;
he gazed intently at Vidura as he was walking away in silence.
Turning suddenly toward the hermitage, he saw the people.
Only King Yudhiṣṭhira pursued him alone as he entered the formidable forest, appearing and disappearing here and there. "Ho!
Ho! Vidura, I am King Yudhiṣṭhira, your beloved! he called out.
Saying this, the lord of men ran toward him with effort;
then Vidura, the best among the wise, stood in a secluded spot at the edge of that forest, taking refuge beneath a certain tree.
The immensely wise Yudhiṣṭhira recognized that man of great intellect, who was reduced to little more than a mere physical form,
as he stood before him and said the words, "I am Yudhiṣṭhira."
In the hearing of Vidura, the king replied with a sign;
then, becoming unwinking, he gazed intently at the king,
Vidura having fixed his concentrated vision upon him through his own gaze.
The wise Vidura entered [the body of the king], his limbs indeed entering the limbs;
placing his vital breaths into the vital breaths and his senses into the senses,
he resorted to the power of yoga and entered the body of the monarch.
Vidura, as if blazing with the splendor of Dharmarāja,
was there; the king then beheld Vidura’s body leaning against a tree, his eyes fixed in that very manner, devoid of consciousness.
Then the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja, possessed of great splendor and endowed with knowledge, O lord of the people, considered himself powerful and possessed of many virtues,
and he recalled all that was his own from former times.
The highly effulgent Dharmarāja, desiring to have that *yogadharma*— as it was told by Vyāsa— performed there, became intent on cremating him; then, at that moment, a voice spoke to the learned one.
"O King, this body known as Vidura must not be burned; this is your eternal duty. It must not be burned, it must not be burned, O King—this man of great asceticism."
For one whose body has been consumed by knowledge, there is no further burning.
O King, his worlds shall be named Saṃtānaka;
having attained the dharma of an ascetic, he is not to be grieved for, O scorcher of the foe.
Having been addressed thus, that Dharmarāja returned from there once more and reported all of that to King Vaicitravīrya.
Then that radiant king and all those people at that time—
Bhīmasena and the others were filled with supreme wonder.
Having heard that, the king became joyful and spoke to the son of Dharma.
Then the aged Kuru king spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O King, let these roots and fruits of mine be accepted;
for it is said that whatever food a man eats, O King, his guest is considered to eat the same.
Thus addressed, the son of Dharma replied "So be it" to the king.
Together with his younger brothers, he ate the fruits and roots provided by the king.
Then, having taken up residence at the foot of trees,
they all spent that night subsisting on fruits, roots, and water.
15,034.001 Vaiśampāyana said: O Bhārata, thus did that auspicious night, endowed with the stars, pass for those of meritorious deeds in their hermitage.
In various places, they held conversations characterized by righteousness and worldly purpose, employing a diverse range of expressions and endowed with manifold scriptural citations.
Meanwhile, the Pāṇḍavas then slept upon the ground all around their mother.
O lord of men, having abandoned their most costly beds,
those heroic men dwelt that night eating whatever food the high-minded King Dhṛtarāṣṭra took.
When the night had passed,
however, the son of Kuntī, having performed his morning rites, together with his brothers, his harem,
his attendants, and his family priest, beheld the circle of hermitages.
At his ease and according to his destination, by the permission of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
he beheld there sacrificial altars upon which fires were blazing brightly,
attended by sages who had performed their ablutions and offered oblations into the fire.
Adorned with clusters of wild flowers and rising incense from clarified butter,
they were endowed with a divine, Brahmic splendor and accompanied by throngs of sages; there,
herds of deer rested here and there, free from agitation.
O Lord, it was filled with flocks of birds that seemed to sing without fear,
with the cries of peacocks, the warbling of water-hens,
and the auspicious, ear-pleasing cooing of cuckoos.
In some places it was adorned with the sounds of twice-born men reciting their prayers,
and in others it was graced by great heaps of gathered fruits and roots;
then the king presented those items he had brought for the sake of the ascetics.

O King, the lord of the earth [offered] 15,034.012c golden jars as well as those made of udumbara wood; 15,034.013a antelope skins and woven cloths, and the large and small sacrificial ladles; 15,034.013c likewise water-pots, cooking vessels, and pans, O Bhārata.
O King, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, gave him all of that— iron vessels and various kinds of bowls— whatever he desired, in whatever quantity, and whatever else was wished for.
Thus that righteous king, having circumambulated the circle of hermitages and distributed all that wealth, the lord of the earth returned once more.
And when the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra had performed his daily rites—
Then the righteous-souled one beheld him sitting composedly together with Gāndhārī,
and he saw his mother Kuntī standing nearby, ever-practicing dharma, bowed down like a disciple.
Having honored that king and announced his own name,
he sat down upon a grass mat, being permitted by the words, "Be seated.
Bhīmasena and the other Pāṇḍavas likewise [honored] the bull of the Kauravas.
Having offered salutations and clasped his feet, they sat down by the king's command.
Surrounded by them, that Kuru king shone exceedingly,
bearing a radiant Brahmanic splendor like Bṛhaspati among the gods.
While they were thus seated, the great ṛṣis,
led by Śatayūpa and others who dwelt in Kurukṣetra, arrived;
as did the venerable brahmin Vyāsa, who is honored by the hosts of celestial ṛṣis.
Surrounded by his disciples, the one of great splendor revealed himself to that king.
Then that Kuru king, the heroic son of Kuntī,
and Bhīmasena and the others, rose up and paid him homage.
Then Vyāsa, surrounded by Śatayūpa and others, arrived;
he addressed King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, saying,
"Be seated," upon a new seat made of kuśa grass, covered with a black antelope skin and topped with more kuśa grass.
Then Vyāsa took his place upon that seat which had been prepared for him;
and all those best of the twice-born, endowed with great luster, sat down on their respective seats on every side, having received the permission of Dvaipāyana.
15,035.001 Vaiśampāyana said: When the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were thus seated,
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, addressed the king and spoke.
"O mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra, does your asceticism increase?
O lord of men, does your mind find pleasure in dwelling in the forest? O King, is there no grief in your heart born from the destruction of your sons?"
O sinless one, I hope that all your faculties are serene;
I hope that you practice the forest-dweller's rule, having made your intellect firm;
and I hope that your daughter-in-law Gāndhārī is not overwhelmed by grief.
"Is this queen, who possesses great wisdom and intelligence, who perceives the meaning of the Dharma, and who knows the truth of the coming and going of all things, free from grief? And,
O King, is Kuntī, who serves you without pride, well?"
"Having renounced her own kingdom, she is devoted to the service of her elders;
has King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, been greeted by you with affection? And have Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins also been comforted by you?"
"Do you rejoice upon seeing these? Is your mind stainless? O lord of men, are you pure in nature and have you attained knowledge?
For this triad, O Bhārata, is the most excellent among all beings."
"O Great King, freedom from enmity, truthfulness, and indeed non-malice—
do you perhaps feel no regret, O Bhārata, regarding your dwelling in the forest? Does the forest food taste well to you, O Lord, as do the garments of the sages?"
"O King, it is also known to me by what means the high-souled Vidura departed— that Dharma himself, the great-souled one,
became Vidura due to the curse of Māṇḍavya."
Possessing great intelligence, a great yogi, a high-souled one of vast mind—
whether it be Bṛhaspati among the gods or Śukra among the asuras,
neither was endowed with such wisdom as that bull among men.
Having expended a very great amount of ascetic power accumulated over a long time,
the eternal Dharma was indeed overcome by the seer Māṇḍavya;
formerly, at the command of Brahmā and by my own power, it was thus.
Born in the field of Vicitravīrya,
that one of great intelligence is your brother, O Great King— the eternal god of gods whom the wise know as Dharma, through the meditation on and the maintenance of the highest good.
By truth, self-restraint, and observance of vows, by non-violence, charity, and austerity, the eternal one caused him to grow;
through the power of yoga, he was born as Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus.
"O King, this is what is called Dharma by the wise one of immeasurable intellect:
that Hari, who consists of consciousness, was worshipped by him directly within his own mind;
and having been previously propitiated with devotion by that pure-hearted man through his zeal."
Just as fire, or wind, or water, or earth,
or space, so too does Dharma abide both here and in the hereafter;
and it is all-pervading, O Kauravya, having permeated everything mobile and immobile.
That God of gods is seen by the Siddhas whose sins have been burnt away. For he who is Dharma is Vidura, and he who is Vidura is the son of Pāṇḍu.
O King, this very son of Pāṇḍu stands before you as one submissive, like a servant.
Your brother, the best among the wise, having entered his own self by means of the power of great yoga, has fortunately [reunited] with the high-souled son of Kuntī,
O bull of the Bharatas; and I too shall soon unite you with the highest good.
"Know, my son, that I have come here for the purpose of cutting through your doubts.
I shall show you the wondrous fruit of asceticism— a deed never before performed in this world by any of the great seers."
"O protector of the earth, what superhuman thing do you wish to obtain from me?
Whether it be to see, touch, or hear—speak, and I shall make it so.
Janamejaya said:
O Brahmin, when King Dhṛtarāṣṭra— that tiger among kings— had gone to dwell in the forest together with his wife and his daughter-in-law Kuntī,
and when Vidura had also attained perfection and taken refuge with Dharmarāja;
While all the sons of Pāṇḍu were dwelling within that circle of hermitages,
the great seer Vyāsa, possessed of supreme splendor, said, "I shall indeed perform that which is truly wonderful. Tell me that.

O twice-born one, for how long did Yudhiṣṭhira, the descendant of Kuru and lord of men, dwell in the forest with his followers, O Acyuta? And what was their food, O Lord, as they lived there together with their army?
"O sinless one, tell me why those great-souled ones remained there with their inner apartments.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, [regarding] Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the earth, who had gone to dwell in the forest..."

Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by his brothers and his army, advanced to see him. O bull of the Bharata race, on their first day there, their food consisted of water, roots, and fruits, and they slept upon the ground.

O King, having been thus permitted by the Kuru king, those Pāṇḍavas then rested and enjoyed various kinds of food and drink. For one month, they sported in the forest together with their army and their women of the inner apartments.
Then, O sinless one, Vyāsa arrived there just as I have described to you. While they were all seated near the king in conversation with Vyāsa, O monarch, other sages arrived.
O Bhārata, the high-minded [king] also offered worship, according to the prescribed rules, to Nārada, Parvata, Devala of great asceticism, Viśvāvasu, Tumburu, and Citrasena.
Permitted by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus,
and all those others, having received honors from Yudhiṣṭhira,
then sat down upon auspicious seats covered with sacred kusha grass and excellent cushions.
When they had all taken their seats there, that high-minded king, the best of the Kurus, sat down surrounded by the sons of Pāṇḍu;
and likewise Gāndhārī, Kuntī, Draupadī, and the daughter of the Sātvatas.
Then other women likewise sat down together with others.
O King, their conversations there were divine and most righteous,
concerning the ancient seers and interspersed with accounts of the gods and asuras.

Then, at the conclusion of the discourse, Vyāsa— the best among speakers, possessed of great splendor, and the foremost of all knowers of the Vedas— being pleased, spoke these words once again to that Lord whose eye is wisdom.
"O Indra among kings, that which you desire to speak in your heart is known to me— specifically,
the grief with which you are indeed burning on account of your sons,
O monarch, as well as the sorrow that dwells in the heart of Gāndhārī."
O great king, that which dwells in the hearts of Kuntī and Draupadī,
and that intense grief born of the destruction of their sons which Subhadrā, the sister of Kṛṣṇa, bears— that too is known to me.
"O King, having heard of this assembly of all of you,
I have come here, O delighter of the Kurus, to sever your doubts;
I have arrived, O tiger among the Kurus, to resolve your uncertainties."
"Let these gods, gandharvas, and all the great ṛṣis behold today the power of my asceticism accumulated over a long time.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, tell me: what desire shall I grant you?"
"I am inclined to grant you a boon; behold the power of my asceticism.
Thus addressed by Vyāsa of immeasurable intellect, that lord of kings reflected for a moment and then began to speak.
"I am blessed, I am favored, and my life has become fruitful,
since today I have met with you, the virtuous ones.
And today I also perceive that the desired goal for myself in this world has been attained."

"O you whose wealth is asceticism, since I have been joined by you who are like Brahmā himself, I am purified merely by the sight of you; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, O sinless ones, I have no fear regarding the next world."
But my mind, longing for my son, is constantly tormented as I remember that dull-witted man of evil intellect and his many misdeeds—
by whom the sinless Pāṇḍavas were treated with such cruelty.
This entire earth, along with its men and elephants, has been suddenly struck down;
and high-souled kings, lords of various realms,
having come for the sake of my son, have all fallen under the power of death.
"O Brahmin, what is the destiny of those who were slain in battle for the sake of their friends? Likewise, what is the fate of my sons and grandsons who have been killed in the fray?
My mind is constantly tormented by having caused the death of those of such great strength."
The aged Bhīṣma, son of Śantanu, and Droṇa, the best of the twice-born—
these have been brought to destruction by my foolish, sinful son, who hates his friends and desires the sovereignty of the earth, thereby ruining his illustrious lineage.
"Recalling all this, burning day and night,
struck down by suffering and grief, I find no peace. O father, as I reflect thus, there is no comfort for me."
15,037.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
15,037.001a Having heard that various lamentation of the royal sage,
15,037.001c Gāndhārī’s grief was renewed once more, O Janamejaya.
Then Gāndhārī, overcome with grief for her sons, spoke these words concerning Kuntī, the daughter of Drupada, Subhadrā, and those other excellent women who were the daughters-in-law of the Kuru king.
With her eyes bound, the queen stood with palms joined in reverence;
"O giver of honor, this man longs for his sons who have gone to another world.
O Blessed One, that thought of his was known by you through your ascetic power.
"O bull among sages, sixteen years have passed;
O Lord, there is no peace for this king as he grieves for his slain sons. Indeed, this ruler of the earth sighs, overwhelmed by sorrow for his children."
O great sage, Dhṛtarāṣṭra has not slept through all these nights;
you are capable, by the power of your asceticism, of creating other entire worlds—
how much more so to show the king his sons who have gone to another world?

"And this Draupadī Kṛṣṇā, whose kinsmen and sons have been slain, grieves exceedingly; she is a virtuous woman, your beloved daughter-in-law among daughters-in-law. Likewise is Subhadrā, the sister of Kṛṣṇa, who speaks auspiciously."
"Tormented by the slaughter of Subhadrā’s son, this spirited woman grieves intensely. And this wife of Bhūriśravas,
O Lord, being exceedingly distressed and afflicted by the grief of her husband’s calamity, does not sleep at night."
His father-in-law was the wise Bāhlīka, that upholder of the Kuru lineage,
who was slain along with Somadatta and his own father in the great battle; and he himself was illustrious, possessed of great intelligence, and never fled from combat.
"Since your hundred sons have been slain upon the field of battle,
these hundred wives of his— stricken by grief for their sons—
are increasing the sorrow of the king and of me as well, again and again."
O great sage, because of that great undertaking, he attends upon me;
and as for those high-souled heroes, my fathers-in-law who were great chariot-warriors,
such as Somadatta and the others— what, O Lord, has become of their destiny?
"O Blessed One, through your grace, may this lord of the earth be free from sorrow;
may he, as well as I, Kuntī, and your daughter-in-law here, meet our end [in due time].
When Gāndhārī had spoken thus, Kuntī’s face became emaciated by her vows.
He remembered that son born in secret, who was begotten by the Sun;
and the boon-granting seer Vyāsa, possessing the power of distant hearing and sight,
beheld the queen, the mother of Savyasācin, in her state of distress.
Then Vyāsa said to her: "O highly wise lady, speak that which you desire to say and what is in your mind regarding the task you wish to perform.
Then Kuntī, having bowed her head to her parents-in-law, spoke.
15,037.018c She spoke these words with bashfulness, revealing the ancient [secret]. 15,038.001 Kuntī said:
15,038.001a "O Blessed One, you are my father-in-law; you are even the deity of my deity."
"O God beyond gods, listen to my truthful words:
a certain ascetic Brahmin named Durvāsas, who was prone to anger, came to my father’s house seeking alms to eat, and I gratified him."

"By means of purity, by the abandonment of offenses, and likewise with a pure mind, I shall never become angry even on occasions of great provocation. Being pleased, he granted me this boon; "It is done," I replied.
"Delighted, that great sage, who had accomplished his purpose, became a granter of boons to me;
he spoke these words to me: 'You must certainly accept it.
Trembling with fear, I entreated that twice-born man with humility."
Then, out of fear of the curse, I spoke once more to that brahmin;
and that twice-born man spoke to me again, saying, "So be it.
"O blessed one, O lovely-faced lady, you shall become the mother of Dharma."
"Those gods whom you shall summon will remain under your control. Having spoken thus, the brahmin vanished; I was then filled with wonder, yet my memory did not fail me in any circumstance.
Then, standing upon the roof of the palace, as I gazed at the rising sun and recalled those words of the seer, I longed for the maker of day;
remaining there in my youthful state, I was unaware of the transgression.
Then the thousand-rayed god appeared near me;
dividing his body into two parts, both on the earth and in the sky,
he scorched the worlds with one part and approached me with the second.
He said to me as I was trembling, "Choose a boon from me;
you may go. Bowing my head to him, I replied, "O you of fierce rays, it is not right for you to grant my summons in vain."
"I shall consume both you and the brahmin by whom this boon was granted to you.
"Protecting that innocent brahmin from the curse, I then said:
'O God, may there be a son for me who is equal to you.'"
Then the radiant one, having entered me with his splendor and having deluded me,
said, "A son shall be born to you," and departed for heaven. Thereupon, I remained within my father’s palace, guarding the secret of what had occurred.
"O Brahmin, as a young girl secretly born, I cast Karṇa into the water;
yet surely by the grace of that very god,
I have become a maiden once again, just as that ṛṣi told me."
"Though I knew it was my son, I neglected him out of delusion;
that, O brahmin-sage, consumes me, as is well known to you.
Whether it be sinful or sinless, this matter has been disclosed by me."
"O Blessed One, you ought to dispel this fear of mine here.
And whatever is known to this king and dwells within his heart, O sinless one— may he obtain that desire this very day, O best of sages."
Thus addressed, Vyāsa, the best among those who know the Vedas, replied:
"Excellent! All this is true; it is exactly as you have told me to me.
For the sake of maintaining stability, your intellect has been transformed by that God."
There is no fault in you, for you have attained the state of a maiden;
indeed, the gods, who possess sovereign power, do enter into bodies.
There are also hosts of gods who bring forth offspring through mere volition.
"Through speech, sight, touch, and friction—it is fivefold. Human nature is indeed not joined with divine nature;
know this, O Kuntī, and let the fever of your mind depart."
"Everything is wholesome for the powerful; everything is pure for the powerful;
everything is dharma for the powerful; everything belongs to the powerful.
Vyāsa said:
"O blessed Gāndhārī, you shall see your sons, brothers, and friends,
as well as your daughters-in-law together with their husbands, like those who have risen from sleep at night.
And Kuntī shall see Karṇa, and the Yādava woman shall see the son of Subhadrā."
“Draupadī, my five sons, and likewise my fathers and brothers—
this resolve had already been formed in my heart long ago, just as I was urged by the King and by you, Pṛthā.”

"Those high-souled ones, all of them bulls among men, are not to be grieved for; for, being devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriyas, they have thus met their end. That deed of the gods, O blameless lady, was destined to happen inevitably."
Then all of them descended to the surface of the earth with their respective divine portions:
the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Piśācas, Guhyakas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as the Puṇyajanas, the Siddhas, and the celestial ṛṣis.
The gods, the Dānavas, and likewise the stainless Brahmarṣis—
all these have met their end on the field of battle at Kurukṣetra.
And he who was the wise king of the Gandharvas, known as Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
In the world of men, he is your husband Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Know Pāṇḍu to be the most distinguished and infallible among the Maruts. Vidura was a portion of Dharma, as was this King Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Know Kali to be Duryodhana, and likewise know Śakuni to be Dvāpara.
Know Duḥśāsana and the others to be Rākṣasas, O lady of auspicious appearance. Know Bhīmasena, the subduer of foes and possessor of great strength, to have arisen from the host of Maruts."
And know that this Nara-ṛṣi, Pārtha Dhananjaya,
is Nārāyaṇa Hṛṣīkeśa; and that both the Aśvins,
born as twins, are he who, having divided his own body into two, became the Sun, the best of those who give heat.
"Know, O beautiful one, that Karṇa is indeed scorching the worlds; know him,
O auspicious lady of lovely appearance, as the sun who has arisen for the sake of enmity and who generates such intense rivalry."
And he who was the heir of the Pāṇḍavas, slain by six great chariot-warriors—
that Saubhadra was Soma himself, who here became twofold through yoga;
and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who was born from the fire together with Draupadī.
Know that Śubha is a portion of Agni, while Śikhaṇḍin is of the Rākṣasas.
Know that Droṇa is a portion of Bṛhaspati, and the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman) is born of Rudra.
And know Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā, to be a Vasu who has entered into human form.
Gāṅgeya, by means of his divine potency, was a god who had attained human form.
Thus, O highly wise one, these gods, having come to the state of humanity,
returned once more to heaven after their auspicious task was accomplished.
"That sorrow which has long remained in the hearts of you all,
I shall today dispel from the fear caused by the world beyond.
All of you, go toward the river Bhāgīrathī."
"There you shall see all those who have been slain on this field of battle.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of Vyāsa, all the people then...
With a great lion-roar, he proceeded toward the Gaṅgā;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, accompanied by his ministers, set out together with the Pāṇḍavas,
joined by the tigers among sages and the assembled Gandharvas.

Then, having reached the Gaṅgā in due course, that ocean of people made camp everywhere according to their preference and at their ease. And the king, together with his followers and the Pāṇḍavas, stayed in a chosen location.
The wise one made his dwelling there, preceded by women and elders;
and that day passed for them as if it were a hundred years,
as they awaited the night, longing to see the deceased kings.
Then, as the sun reached the auspicious western mountain,
they performed their evening rites after having completed their ablutions.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, when night had arrived, all those who were assembled there, having performed their evening rites, approached Vyāsa. Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the righteous-souled one, was then together with the Pāṇḍavas.
Pure and single-minded, he sat down together with those sages;
the women, along with Gāndhārī, sat down together as well,
as did all the people of the city and the countryside, each according to their age.
Then the great sage Vyāsa, possessed of great splendor, having immersed himself in the holy waters of the Bhāgīrathī, summoned all the worlds,
as well as all the warriors of the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas from every side.
And the highly fortunate kings dwelling in various lands, O Janamejaya,
all stood waiting in expectation of their arrival;
then, O Janamejaya, a tumultuous sound arose from within the water.
15,040.006c It appeared just as before between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
15,040.007a Then all those kings, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa,
rose up from that water by the thousands, together with their armies.
Both Virāṭa and Drupada, together with their sons and their armies; the sons of Draupadī, the son of Subhadrā, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca;
and both Karṇa and Duryodhana, as well as the great car-warrior Śakuni.
And Duḥśāsana and the other great car-warriors among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
as well as the son of Jarāsaṃdha, Bhagadatta, King Jalasaṃdha,
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, and Vṛṣasena with his younger brother.
Prince Lakṣmaṇa, the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
all the sons of Śikhaṇḍin, Dhṛṣṭaketu with his younger brother,
as well as Acala, Vṛṣaka, and the Rākṣasa Alāyudha.
Bāhlīka, Somadatta, and Cekitāna the king—
these and many others who were not mentioned due to their great number—
all rose up from the water with radiant bodies.
Whatever the attire, whatever the banner, and whatever the vehicle of each hero, by those very things the lords of men were seen;
with whatever armor and whatever weapon [each possessed], he was seen by means of that very thing.
All of them were clad in celestial garments, all wore radiant earrings,
and were free from enmity, free from egoism, and devoid of anger and resentment;
they were being sung to by Gandharvas and praised by bards.

Wearing celestial garlands and garments, and surrounded by throngs of Apsarases— O lord of men, the sage who is the son of Satyavatī, being pleased, then bestowed divine vision upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra through the power of his asceticism.
The illustrious Gāndhārī, endowed with the power of divine knowledge,
beheld all those sons as well as others who had been slain in battle. That was a wonderful, inconceivable, and exceedingly hair-raising sight.
All those people, filled with wonder, gazed with unblinking eyes upon that army as it approached—
exhilarated by the intoxication of the festival and crowded with joyful men and women—
appearing like a vivid scene depicted on a canvas.
But Dhṛtarāṣṭra, beholding them all with his divine eye,
rejoiced, O best of the Bharatas, through the grace of that sage.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then those best of the Bharatas came together with one another,
all their anger and envy gone, and all their impurities removed;
they followed the supreme and auspicious rite ordained by the Brahman-sages.
With hearts full of joy, like the immortals in the world of the gods,
O King, they were all gathered together: son with father and mother, wife with husband, brother with brother, and friend with friend.
The Pāṇḍavas, along with the sons of Draupadī, all rushed forward with great joy toward the great archer Karṇa and the son of Subhadrā; meanwhile,
Duryodhana, having saluted the King of Dharma, fell to the ground.
Having firmly embraced Suyodhana along with his brothers, Karṇa, accompanied by his own uterine brothers,
first saluted his feet.
Having honored Bhīṣma and all the others, he stood there;
having embraced Dharmarāja, Bhīma, and the twins,
he also clasped his uterine brother Pṛṣata and Jiṣṇu in a very firm embrace.
Having comforted Draupadī, Subhadrā, and his own queen, the son of Subhadrā— the hero— stood there gazing at his son Parikṣit. Then the Pāṇḍavas, together with Karṇa, were indeed filled with joy.
Having come together, the protectors of the earth remained established in friendship.
O bull of the Bharatas, having met one another, those warriors—
and other kṣatriyas as well— had their anger dispelled through the grace of the ṛṣis.
Having abandoned hostility and established themselves in friendship,
all these tigers among men— the Kurus and other humans— have thus assembled together with their elders, kinsmen, and sons.

Having spent that entire single night with delighted minds, those kings considered themselves, through their satisfaction, to be like dwellers in heaven. Herein there was no sorrow, no fear, no terror, no discontent, and no infamy.
O bull of the Bharatas, having come together with one another among the warriors,
those women— having been reunited with their fathers, brothers, husbands, and sons— attained the highest joy and cast off their sorrow.
Those who have gone to the world of the gods, and those who have gone to the assembly of Brahmā;
those who have reached the world of Varuṇa, and those who have taken refuge in Goloka;
likewise, those who have gone to the world of Vaivasvata, and those who have approached the Yakṣas.
The Rākṣasas, the Piśācas, and likewise the people of the Northern Kurus,
as well as others who had attained various diverse destinies and were driven by their karma— all of them arrived there, possessing the same age, form, and dress.
And those kings who had resorted to the Gandharva realm— those heroes and their women— having thus spent a single night with those who perform meritorious deeds, [departed].
Having addressed one another and embraced, they then departed as they had come.
Then that bull among sages dismissed those people;
and even as they were looking on, they vanished in an instant.
Having plunged into the holy river that flows through the three worlds, those great-souled ones,
together with their chariots and banners, returned to their own abodes;
some went to the world of the gods, and others likewise to the assembly of Brahmā.
Some reached the world of Varuṇa, and some attained the realm of Kubera;
likewise, some kings reached the world of Vaivasvata,
and some even the land of the Uttarakurus, along with the Rākṣasas and Piśācas.
All those high-souled ones, together with the gods, arrived by various means of travel, accompanied by their mounts and followers.
When they had all departed, the great sage remained standing in the water.
Virtuous in character, possessed of great splendor, and always intent on the welfare of the Kurus,
he then spoke to all those Kṣatriya women whose lords had been slain: "Whichever of you excellent women desire the worlds attained by husbands..."
"Let them, therefore, without delay, plunge into the waters of the Jahnavī.
Hearing these words of his, those excellent women, full of faith,
obtained their father-in-law's permission and entered the waters of the Jahnavī.
Then, having bestowed their northern regions [upon their sons] and having obtained the consent of their own sons,
and having likewise obtained the consent of Bhūriśravas, Droṇa,
and the others, they were liberated from their human bodies along with their husbands.
O lord of the people, at that time all those virtuous women gathered together;
in this manner, all those well-behaved women of noble family [spoke], saying: "Go always with your husbands."
Then, O King, those Kṣatriya women whose lords had been slain entered the water and, being liberated, attained the same world as their husbands;
they were endowed with divine forms and adorned with celestial ornaments.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, just like their husbands, they—
endowed with virtue and courage, free from darkness and fatigue,
and all possessed of every excellence— each reached her own respective abode.
At that time, whatever desire each individual had,
Vyāsa— the granter of boons and lover of dharma— granted it all.
Having heard that the kings of men were to return once more, the people...
They rejoiced and were filled with joy, even those who had passed into other bodies;
having seen that supreme marvel, all the Paurava men became free from the conception of fear and cleansed of all taint.
The man who hears this account of their reunion with those they love will always obtain pleasant things both in this world and after death—
reunion with beloved kinsmen, free from toil and free from disease.
The wise man who causes this to be heard shall attain supreme perfection;
he shall obtain glory in this world and a blessed state in the hereafter. O Bhārata, those men who are devoted to sacred study and engaged in ritual action [attain these].
Men of virtuous conduct, endowed with self-control, whose sins have been shaken off by giving; who are upright, pure, and tranquil, free from violence and falsehood;
and who are devoted to the yoga of the inner self and possessed of fortitude.
They have appeared again and have been proclaimed once more;
repeatedly they always bestow fearlessness upon those who hear them. By constantly hearing this sacred section (*parvan*), they shall attain the supreme goal.
15,042.001 Sūta said: Having heard this account of the coming and going of all his ancestors at that time, the wise King Janamejaya was filled with joy.
And filled with joy, he spoke again regarding their return:
"How indeed can there be a vision of that form once they have abandoned their bodies?
Thus addressed, that powerful disciple of Vyāsa, the best of the twice-born, replied.
The best among speakers addressed King Janamejaya:
"O King, it is the settled conclusion that there is no destruction of any actions;
bodies and likewise physical forms are born of action."
The great elements are eternal because they rely upon the Lord of Beings;
their association is perpetual, and there is no destruction when they are separated. Action is performed for the sake of non-destruction, and the arrival of its fruit is desired by him.
The self, when joined with these [qualities], experiences pleasure and pain;

yet it is indestructible and eternal—this is the certainty regarding the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). For those who possess true knowledge, that essential nature of the self which exists within all beings is indeed constant.
As long as karma is not exhausted, so long does it maintain its own nature;
once his karma is completely exhausted, the person attains a change of form.
Having entered a body, various states of being and oneness become united.

For those who understand the state of distinctness, these [elements] are likewise eternal. Regarding the immolation of the horse in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, there is this Vedic revelation: "The vital breaths have gone to another world; for the horses are indeed eternal."
"O King, I speak this for your benefit, provided it is pleasing to you. For you have heard of the paths leading to the gods during the performance of sacrifices;
where your sacrifice is well-performed, there the gods are well-disposed toward you."

When the gods are endowed with this [knowledge], they become masters over the movement of sacrificial animals; having attained such a state through sacrifice, they do not become anything other than eternal. A man who [realizes this] within this eternal group of five and within the eternal Self—

The fool who perceives the various combinations of this [body] in vain will grieve excessively at their separation; such is my view. He who sees the fault in separation should avoid union in this world.
In the unattached there is no attachment, nor is there the suffering born of separation on this earth.
But the man who knows both the higher and the lower is not stirred by pride;
knowing the lower and touching the higher intellect, he is liberated from delusion.
Having emerged from the unseen, he has again gone to the unseen;
I do not know him, nor does he know me, and yet there is no detachment in me. With whatever body this powerless one acts, [so it is].
By whichever body one possesses, one necessarily experiences that [result]:
with the mind one attains what is mental, and possessing a body, one attains what is physical.
Vaiśampāyana said:

O best of the Kurus, having not seen his sons before, the king obtained a vision of them in their true forms through the grace of the ṛṣi. That king [learned] the duties of kings as well as the Brahma-Upaniṣad.
The best of men attained both spiritual realization and certainty of intellect;
and the highly wise Vidura achieved perfection through the power of asceticism,
as did Dhṛtarāṣṭra upon approaching the ascetic Vyāsa.
Janamejaya said:
"If Vyāsa, the granter of boons, would show me my father as well—
in his same form, dress, and age— then I would believe everything you have told me."
"It would be dear to me, and I would have my purpose fulfilled, having made this firm resolve. By the grace of the son of the seer, may my desire be realized.
Sūta said:

When the king had spoken these words, the powerful and wise Vyāsa showed him favor and brought back Parīkṣit. Then [he beheld] the monarch, returned from heaven, possessing the same form and age as before.
King Janamejaya beheld his illustrious father,
the high-souled Śamīka, as well as that son of his, Śṛṅgin,
and he also saw those who had been the king’s ministers.
Then, at the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*), King Janamejaya was filled with joy;
he caused his father to bathe, and the monarch himself bathed as well.
Having bathed, O best of the Bharatas, that king spoke thus to Āstīka:
"O Āstīka, born of the Yāyāvara lineage, son of Jaratkāru,
it is my conviction that this sacrifice is full of various wonders,
since today this father of mine has arrived, the destroyer of my grief."
Āstīka said:
O best of the Kuru lineage, at that sacrifice where the sage Dvaipāyana— the ancient treasury of ascetic power— was present, both worlds were conquered by him.
"O delighter of the Pāṇḍavas, you have heard this wonderful narrative;
the serpents were reduced to ashes and followed the path of their father. By some means, O King, Takṣaka was released because of your truthfulness."
All the sages were honored after witnessing the destiny of that high-souled one;
having heard this account which destroys sin, a vast merit was attained,
and the knot of the heart was loosened by the sight of such noble persons.
"Those who uphold the side of Dharma and those who delight in virtuous conduct— to them, upon seeing whom evil wanes, one should offer salutations.
Sūta said:
Having heard this from the best of the twice-born, King Janamejaya—
Vaiśampāyana said—
beheld his deceased father and paid homage to that sage.
Through the grace of that sage, the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra honored that ṛṣi,
showing him reverence again and again; and Parīkṣit also vanished right there.
Janamejaya, the knower of dharma, asked that steadfast sage Vaiśampāyana, O best of men, about the remainder of the narrative concerning the forest exile. Janamejaya said:
"Having seen his sons, as well as his grandsons and their followers, what did King Dhṛtarāṣṭra do, O lord of men, and what did King Yudhiṣṭhira do?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having witnessed that great marvel— the sight of his sons once again—
that royal seer was freed from sorrow and returned to his hermitage;
so too did all the other people and those supreme ṛṣis.
By the permission of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, they departed as they pleased;
but the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, accompanied by a very small force of soldiers,
followed that great-souled lord of the earth together with his wives.
When he had reached the hermitage, the wise Brahman-sage, honored by the world, the seer who was the son of Satyavatī, approached King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and spoke these words to him;
having arrived, Dvaipāyana addressed the king thus.
"O mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O delighter of the Kauravas, listen!
You have heard from sages who are advanced in knowledge, performers of meritorious deeds,
and who are distinguished by their prosperity and noble lineage, as well as those who are knowers of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas."
15,044.007c As those ancient knowers of dharma spoke various stories,
[they told] how this Vāsudeva, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, by his very power,
[is the Lord of the World], and how Dharma remains in the world even during the Kali age.
By his grace, may this great king attain righteousness;
by the touch of his lotus feet, may Kali not reach this earth. Do not set your mind on grief; the wise man is not distressed by destiny.

"You have heard from Nārada, who has the vision of the gods, this secret of the deities. By following the duty of a Kṣatriya, your sons have attained that auspicious state purified by weapons, just as you saw them wandering according to their will."
"This wise Yudhiṣṭhira, together with all his brothers, his wives, and his circle of friends, awaits your command. Grant him leave; let him go to rule over his own kingdom."
"Indeed, more than thirteen months have passed while they were dwelling in the forest.
O scorcher of foes, this position must always be guarded with great effort;
for this thing called 'kingdom,' O lord of men, has many adversaries."
Thus addressed by Vyāsa of immeasurable intellect, the Kuru king, being eloquent, summoned Yudhiṣṭhira and spoke these words:
"O Ajātaśatru, may prosperity be yours; listen to me along with your brothers."
"O protector of the earth, by your grace, grief no longer oppresses us.
O wise one, I rejoice with you, my son, just as before in Hastināpura, followed by you, my lord, who remain devoted to what is pleasing."
"I have obtained the fruit of a son from you; my affection for you is great. O mighty-armed one, I harbor no anger toward you; go, my son, do not delay.
Seeing you here, my ascetic merit is being diminished."
"Seeing you, whose body is endowed with ascetic power, my own body has been sustained once more.
Likewise, these two mothers of yours, who subsist on withered leaves,
will not remain long, O son, as they observe a vow equal to mine."
Duryodhana and the others, having gone to the other world, have been seen through the power of Vyāsa’s asceticism and through your meeting with him;
O sinless one, the purpose for which I lived has long since been fulfilled.
"I shall undertake fierce asceticism; you ought to grant me permission.
Today, upon you depend the funeral offerings, my reputation, and this entire lineage.
O mighty-armed one, go tomorrow or even today; my son, do not delay."
"O bull of the Bharatas, you have heard the science of statecraft (*rājanīti*) many times. O Lord, I see nothing further that needs to be instructed; this much has been accomplished.
When he had spoken these words, dear one, the king addressed the monarch.
At that time, the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, who knows what is right, spoke words that were both timely and true:
"O knower of dharma, you ought not to abandon me, for I am innocent.
Let all my brothers and followers go as they please."
"I shall seek out you, O one of firm vows, as well as my two mothers.
To him, Gāndhārī then said: "Do not do this, my son; listen to me.
The Kuru lineage and the funeral offerings for my father-in-law depend entirely upon you."
"Go, my son; this much is sufficient, for we have been honored.
O son, you must carry out what the king has said—the word of your father.
Having been addressed thus by Gāndhārī, he spoke these words to Kuntī.
Wiping her eyes, which were clouded with tears and oil, she spoke these words while weeping:
"The King and the illustrious Gāndhārī are dismissing me.
Kuntī said:
"You are emaciated from service, and there is no greater merit for me than this. It is not proper to create an obstacle to your asceticism; we ourselves are weakened by our initiatory vows.
Indeed, at the time of death, it is not fitting to concern oneself with offspring and such things."
"But with my heart bound to you, how shall I depart in such distress?
Nor do I venture to cause an obstacle to your asceticism, O practitioner of dharma;
for there is nothing superior to asceticism, and through asceticism one attains greatness."

"O Queen, my mind is no longer inclined toward the kingdom as it was before; rather, my heart is now devoted with its whole being to asceticism alone. And this entire earth is empty to me, O auspicious one, and brings me no joy."
"Our kinsmen have been utterly destroyed, and our strength is not as it was before.
The Pāñcālas have been greatly diminished; only a single maiden remains among them. O auspicious lady, I do not see anyone among them who can restore their lineage."
Indeed, all [the troops] were reduced to ashes by Drona alone in battle;
those who remained were slain by the son of Drona during the night.
The Chedis and the Matsyas have likewise been seen by us before in this same manner.
The entire circle of the Vṛṣṇis, however, is protected by Vāsudeva;
he always takes pleasure in the aged, and he is that god who is the supreme self. Having seen him, I wish to remain for the sake of dharma and not for any other reason.
"O Śivā, look upon us all; your sight is difficult to obtain.
O Mother, for the king will indeed undertake severe penance.
Having heard this, the mighty-armed Sahadeva, the lord of warriors, [spoke].
With eyes clouded by tears, he said this to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O bull among kings, I cannot bear to abandon my mother.
May you return quickly; I shall perform austerities in the forest."
"Right here I shall wither away my body through asceticism,
intent upon serving at the feet of the king and these two mothers.
Then Kuntī, embracing that mighty-armed one, said to him:
"Go, my son; do not speak thus, but follow my word. May your journeys be auspicious; be at ease, my dear sons.
Otherwise, there would be an obstruction to our ascetic practice."
"Bound by the noose of affection for you, I would fall away from my supreme asceticism;
therefore, my dear son, you must go, for what remains of our time, O Lord, is but little.
Thus was his mind steadied by Kuntī with these various words.
O Indra among kings, especially for King Sahadeva [and his brothers],
those bulls of the Kurus, having been granted permission by their mother and by the king,
paid homage to the best of the Kurus and began to take their leave.
"O King, we shall depart in safety, having been greeted with favor. Command us, O mighty-armed one; we are all followers of your instructions.
Permitted by you, O King, we shall go forth cleansed of sin."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Dharmarāja,
that royal sage greeted Yudhiṣṭhira with blessings of victory and gave him leave to depart;
then the king comforted Bhīma, the foremost of the strong.
The wise and valiant one accepted his command correctly;
and having embraced Arjuna and the twins, those bulls among men,
that descendant of Kuru dismissed them after hugging and congratulating them.
Having been permitted by Gāndhārī and having performed obeisance at her feet, they were smelled upon the head and embraced by their mother; then,
like calves being restrained from leaving, they all circumambulated the king.
Gazing at him again and again, they proceeded to circumambulate him;
likewise, the virtuous Draupadī and all the Kuru women,
having performed their duties toward their father-in-law according to the prescribed rule, then departed.
Permitted by their two mothers-in-law, embraced and congratulated,
and instructed as to what was to be done, they set out with their husbands.
Then there arose the clamor of the charioteers, "Yoke the horses!"
Amidst the braying of camels and the neighing of horses,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his wife, his army,
and his kinsmen, returned once more to the city of Hastināpura.
15,045.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
When two years had passed since the Pāṇḍavas returned, once, by chance,
in the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura), by chance...
O King, the celestial sage Nārada came to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having honored him, the mighty-armed Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira,
the best among speakers, addressed him as he sat there at ease.
The eloquent and wise one, bowing with humility, spoke these words:
"After a long time indeed, I behold the Blessed One arrived before me.
O Brahmin, is all well with you? Has some auspicious fortune presented itself?"
Having offered his salutations, O King, the Pāṇḍava spoke together with his brothers:
"Which regions have been visited by you, and what service may I perform for you? Tell me that, O foremost of the twice-born; you are a beloved guest to us."

15,045.005 Nārada said: "O King, it has been a long time since I have seen you; I have come from the forest of asceticism (tapovana). O monarch, I have visited various sacred fords (tīrthas) as well as the Gaṅgā."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Men dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā tell me today that the high-souled Dhṛtarāṣṭra has undertaken supreme asceticism."
"They say that my eldest father has undertaken supreme asceticism;
having gone there to see that best of kings, I have returned. Have you seen that upholder of the Kuru lineage there, and is he well?"
"Gāndhārī, Pṛthā, and Saṃjaya the son of a Sūta—
how is my father, that king, faring today?
O Blessed One, I wish to hear [this] if the king has been seen by you."
15,045.009 Nārada said:
"O great king, compose yourself and hear everything exactly as it is,
just as it was heard and seen by me in that forest of asceticism."
O joy of the Kurus, O King, while you were returning from your residence in the forest,
your wise father went from Kurukṣetra to Gaṅgādvāra,
accompanied by Gāndhārī and his daughter-in-law Kuntī.

Accompanied by his charioteer Sañjaya, your father Dhṛtarāṣṭra— possessor of ascetic wealth, together with his sacred fires and his officiating priests— undertook intense austerities. Having established himself there in fierce penance, the high-minded Dhṛtarāṣṭra remained steadfast.
Placing a wooden gourd in his mouth, the sage subsisted on air alone;
honored by all the sages in the forest,
that king of great asceticism remained for six months with nothing but skin and bone remaining.
Gāndhārī subsisted on water alone, while Kuntī fasted for a month;
O Bhārata, Saṃjaya sustained himself by eating only every sixth meal.
And there, O Lord, the officiating priests offered oblations into the fires according to the prescribed rites.
