In that forest, the king was sometimes visible and sometimes invisible; then, having no fixed dwelling, he became a wanderer in the woods. And those two queens together, as well as Sañjaya, followed him.
Saṃjaya was the leader of the king on both even and uneven ground;
and, O King, the blameless Pṛthā was the eye for Gāndhārī.
Then, at one time, that best of kings [was] on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā, the wise one set out toward the hermitage. Then a wind arose, and a great forest fire broke out;
it consumed that entire forest, seizing it from all sides.
While herds of deer and double-tongued serpents were being consumed on all sides,
and while herds of boars were seeking refuge in bodies of water—
in that forest thus overwhelmed, a supreme calamity had arrived.
Due to his lack of food, the king’s vital functions were feeble;
he was incapable of moving away, and your two mothers were exceedingly emaciated.
Then that monarch, seeing the fire approaching nearby, [fainted].
Then, O lord of the earth, he said this to the charioteer Sañjaya:
"Go, Sañjaya, to where the fire shall never burn you;
we, joined with the fire here, shall go to the supreme goal."
To him, Sañjaya, the best of speakers, spoke while deeply distressed:
"O King, this death by fire shall come upon you in vain;
yet I see no means for your escape from the consuming flames."
"You ought to tell me what must be done next in this matter.
Thus addressed by Sañjaya, that king spoke again:
"This death is not undesirable for us who have departed from our home of our own accord."
"Water, fire, air, or even emaciation—these are praised for ascetics. Go, Sañjaya, do not delay!
Having spoken thus to Sañjaya, the king then composed his mind.
Facing eastward, he then sat down together with Gāndhārī and Kuntī.
Seeing him thus seated, Sañjaya circumambulated him from left to right;
and the wise man said to him, "O Lord, compose yourself."
The wise son of the seer, that king, carried out those words;
having restrained the collection of his senses, he then sat like a log of wood.
So too did the highly blessed Gāndhārī and your mother Pṛthā.
When [the city] was overtaken by a forest fire, your father, that king,
and the high minister Sañjaya were released from that conflagration;
I saw him on the bank of the Gaṅgā, surrounded by ascetics.
Having taken leave of them and reported all of this in its entirety,
the radiant charioteer Sañjaya departed for the Himavat mountain.
Thus did that high-minded king of the Kurus meet his end.
O lord of men, O bull of the Bharata race, while I was wandering at will, I beheld the body of the king as well as those of both queens, Gāndhārī and Pṛthā, your two mothers.
Then, having heard of the king’s end as well as his final destination, those whose wealth is asceticism gathered in that penance grove; yet they did not grieve.
O best of men, it was there that I heard all of this.
O Pāṇḍava,

O Indra among kings, you should not grieve that the king has been consumed by fire, nor those two queens; for that lord of the earth and your mother Gāndhārī have reached a blessed end through contact with the fire.
15,045.039 Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard this account of the departure of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, a great sorrow arose among all the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.

Then a great cry of distress arose from the women of the inner apartments, and likewise from the citizens, O Great King, upon hearing of the king’s departure. Crying out, "Alas! Woe! the king was overwhelmed with intense grief.
With his arms raised and remembering his mother, Yudhiṣṭhira wept;
and all those brothers, led by Bhīmasena,
likewise wept, tormented by grief as they then described Pṛthā.

Then, within the inner apartments, a very great sound of weeping arose; O Great King, having heard that Pṛthā had thus passed away, a tremendous sound of lamentation manifested throughout the inner quarters.
They all lamented for that aged lord of men, who had been thus consumed by fire and whose sons were slain, as well as for the ascetic Gāndhārī;
and when that noise had subsided after a moment, O Bhārata.
15,045.044c Restraining his tears with fortitude, the King of Dharma spoke this:
15,046.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
15,046.001a "While that great-souled one was thus engaged in such fierce asceticism,"
"Like the death of one who is helpless while we, his kinsmen, are still alive—
such is my view, for the destinies of men are difficult to discern,
since this son of Vicitravīrya has thus been consumed by a forest fire."
He who once possessed a hundred illustrious sons and was mighty-armed,
that king, whose strength equaled ten thousand elephants, has indeed been consumed by a forest fire—
he whom excellent women used to fan with palm-leaf fans in the past.
Vultures are fanning him, who was once surrounded by forest fires;
he who used to be awakened from sleep by throngs of bards and panegyrists now lies upon the earth, a king brought low by the deeds of my own sin.

I do not grieve for the illustrious Gāndhārī, whose sons have been slain; she has attained the world of her husband and remains steadfast in her devotion to him. But I grieve only for Pṛthā, who possessed the prosperous sovereignty of her sons.
Having abandoned that most magnificent and blazing [kingdom], he resolved to dwell in the forest.
"Fie on this sovereignty of ours! Fie on our strength! Fie on our prowess! And fie on the duty of the Kṣatriyas, because we live as if dead!"
"O best among the foremost of the twice-born, the course of time is indeed exceedingly subtle, since she,
the mother of Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and Vijaya, abandoned the kingdom and took pleasure in dwelling in the forest."
Thinking, "How has she been consumed like one who is helpless? I am bewildered with thought.
Savyasācin has gratified the fire in vain at Khāṇḍava;
it is my opinion that he is ungrateful, being unaware of the favor done for him.
15,046.012a Wherein that Blessed One burned the mother of Savyasācin,
15,046.012c having assumed the disguise of a Brahmin and approached him seeking alms— 15,046.012e Fie on Agni! And fie on the renowned truthfulness of Pārtha!
"O Lord, he whose conduct is such as yours has burned my mother.
Moreover, O Blessed One, this other thing appears to me even more painful:
that the lord of the earth met his end through a futile fire."
Thus, how could such a death come to that ascetic royal seer of the Kuru lineage, who had ruled this entire earth,
while his fires— purified by mantras— remained present in the great forest?
"Afflicted by a senseless fire, my father has met his end.
I imagine Prithā, trembling, emaciated, and covered with visible veins, crying out in great terror, 'O dear one! O Dharmarāja!'"
"O Bhīma, protect me from fear! she cried out, wailing thus; "O Bhīma, save me from the terror of the forest fire!"—my mother was surrounded on all sides by that conflagration.
Sahadeva was indeed dearer to her than all her other sons;
yet that hero, the son of Mādravatī, did not release her.
Hearing this, they all wept, embracing one another.
The five Pāṇḍavas, afflicted by grief like the elements at the end of an eon,
were there; and the sound of the weeping of those lords of men,
though obstructed by the expanse of the palace, resounded through both heaven and earth.
Gazing at one another again and again, and remembering the calamity that had befallen their mother,
the kings could not endure it; they fell to the surface of the earth,
and rising once more, they embraced her, weeping with discordant cries.
Out of grief for Dharmarāja, the Pāṇḍavas fell at his feet.
Nārada said:
"He was not burnt by a useless fire, as I have heard there."
"O Bhārata, I shall tell you how King Vaicitravīrya acted:
we have heard that when that wise king entered the forest and subsisted on air alone, he caused the sacrificial fires to perform the ritual and then relinquished them."
Then, O best of the Bharatas, the sacrificial priests abandoned those fires of his in the lonely forest and departed as they pleased.
It is said that the fire then grew large within that forest.
"The ascetics told me that this forest was set ablaze by him;
O bull of the Bharatas, that king was consumed by that very fire on the banks of the Jahnavī, just as I have described to you."
"O sinless Yudhiṣṭhira, those sages whom I saw on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī have thus informed me,
O lord of the earth, that the king has been united with his own fire."

"Do not grieve; you have followed the king, who has attained the supreme goal. And by her service to her elders, O Pāṇḍava, your mother has likewise attained great perfection; of this I have no doubt."
"O descendant of Kuru, you ought to perform the water-rites for them;
together with all your brothers, let this be ordained here.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then that protector of the earth, the leader of the Pāṇḍavas,
O bull of the Bharatas, went forth together with his brothers and his wives;
and the citizens and the people of the countryside also followed, led by their devotion to the king.
Clad in a single garment, they proceeded toward the Gaṅgā;
then, having plunged into the water, all those bulls of the Kuru race,
placing Yuyutsu at their head, offered water to the high-souled one.

Performing the purification rites for Gāndhārī and Pṛthā according to the rules regarding names and lineages, they stayed there outside the city. He then dispatched men who were knowledgeable in the ordinances and capable of executing their tasks.
At Gaṅgādvāra, where the king, the best of the Kurus, had been cremated,
the lord of the earth then commanded his men— who had received their due wages— to establish memorial shrines for them right there at Gaṅgādvāra.
On the twelfth day, having performed his purificatory rites, that lord of men,
the Pāṇḍava, duly offered the Śrāddha ceremonies accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to them;
that sovereign of the earth offered these specifically for the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
He gave gold, silver, cows, and very costly beds—
each separately for Gāndhārī and Pṛthā—
as well as many jewels and various kinds of garments.
The joy of the Kurus gave away various objects of great value;
having proclaimed his names, the king bestowed that unsurpassed gift. Having proclaimed his names, O King, the monarch gave away those gifts.
Whatever a twice-born man desires and however much he desires, that much he obtains; indeed,
as much as the Brahmins desire, so much shall those twice-born ones receive—
bedding, food, vehicles, precious gems, and wealth.
The king, the lord of the earth, bestowed vehicles, garments, enjoyments, female slaves, and attendants, dedicating them to those two mothers.
Then that protector of the world, having performed numerous *śrāddha* rites, [proceeded].
The wise one entered once again the city named Vārāṇasī,
whose streets were sprinkled and swept, adorned with raised banners and arches,
and crowded with joyful and well-fed people at their arrival.
And those men who had gone there at the king's command performed the rites for Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, and Kuntī in groups,
at the auspicious and holy Gaṅgādvāra, just as directed by the high-souled one.
Having performed the funeral rites for them, they returned once more from there; having honored their remains with various garlands and perfumes according to the prescribed rules,
and having united their lineages, they reported this to the lord of the earth.
Having comforted King Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul is devoted to dharma,
Nārada, the supreme ṛṣi, departed as he desired, O King,
for Dvārakā to see Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva Janārdana.
Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace— Nārāyaṇa, the one free from ailment, intent upon revealing the secret doctrine.
In this manner, years passed for the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

During his residence in the forest, he gave gifts for fifteen years; meanwhile, while his son was being slain in battle, he continued to give gifts constantly for ten and five more years to his kinsmen,
relatives, friends, brothers, and his own people.
But King Yudhiṣṭhira, his mind not at all joyful then,
continued to uphold that kingdom with his kinsmen and relatives slain;
likewise, he remained composed even during the Āśramavāsika Parvan.
And one should feed the twice-born with sacrificial food (haviṣya) accompanied by perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
